papers.title: Post-Babesiosis Warm Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia
papers.population_and_n: Retrospective single-centre cohort (Brigham and Women's Hospital), 86 patients with babesiosis (B. microti) diagnosed January 2009 to June 2016; 18 asplenic; 6 developed warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (WAHA).
papers.abstract_summary: Babesiosis usually causes non-immune haemolytic anaemia that resolves with antimicrobial therapy. After noticing sporadic cases of WAHA after treatment, the authors reviewed all babesiosis patients treated at their centre over 7.5 years for haematological complications within 3 months. Of 86 patients, 18 were asplenic. Six developed WAHA 2 to 4 weeks after diagnosis, by which time all had responded clinically and biochemically to antimicrobials and cleared B. microti parasitaemia. All six were asplenic (P<0.001). All had a positive direct antiglobulin test for IgG and complement C3, warm autoantibodies were identified, and no alternative cause of haemolysis was found. Four of the six needed immunosuppressive treatment. None had prior autoimmunity. The authors conclude that post-babesiosis WAHA occurs in people without prior autoimmune disease and that asplenic patients appear at particular risk. (Paraphrased from the PubMed record as returned by WebFetch.)
papers.key_finding: 6 of 86 babesiosis patients (all 6 asplenic) developed IgG/C3-positive warm AIHA 2-4 weeks after parasitaemia cleared; 4 needed immunosuppression.
papers.corrections: PubMed record (efetch XML) has no CommentsCorrectionsList entries: no erratum, retraction or expression of concern. Publication type: Journal Article only. Note this is the only abstract-level human babesiosis cohort; the 6 WAHA cases are numerically small and the cohort is single-centre and retrospective.

papers.title: Cell-free hemoglobin mediated oxidative stress is associated with acute kidney injury and renal replacement therapy in severe falciparum malaria: an observational study
papers.population_and_n: Prospective observational study of adults (Bangladesh): 107 severe falciparum malaria, 80 uncomplicated malaria, 28 sepsis patients.
papers.abstract_summary: The study asked whether cell-free haemoglobin (CFH) drives oxidative stress and kidney injury in severe falciparum malaria. AKI (creatinine at least 1.5 times expected baseline) was present at enrolment in 62 of 107 severe malaria patients (58%). Patients with AKI had higher admission CFH (geometric mean 8.8 vs 5.1 microM, P=0.018), F2-isoprostanes (56.7 vs 27.8 pg/ml, P<0.001) and isofurans (109.2 vs 41.7 pg/ml, P<0.001). CFH correlated with haemolysis markers, parasite burden (PfHRP2) and F2-isoprostanes. F2-isoprostanes and isofurans were higher in patients who later needed haemodialysis and in fatal cases, and F2-isoprostanes correlated inversely with red cell deformability. Over 72 hours, F2-isoprostanes, isofurans, PfHRP2, CFH and red cell rigidity were independently associated with rising creatinine. Admission F2-isoprostanes, isofurans and deformability were associated with later dialysis. (Paraphrased from the PubMed record as returned by WebFetch.)
papers.key_finding: In 107 adults with severe falciparum malaria, cell-free haemoglobin and lipid-peroxidation products (F2-isoprostanes, isofurans) were higher with AKI and tracked later dialysis need and death.
papers.corrections: PubMed record (efetch XML) has no CommentsCorrectionsList entries. Publication type: Journal Article; Observational Study. Abstract does not name haptoglobin, haemopexin or LDH, so it is the CFH/oxidative-injury comparator, not the scavenger-depletion comparator.

papers.title: Dysregulation of the haem-haemopexin axis is associated with severe malaria in a case-control study of Ugandan children
papers.volume_issue_pages: 14:511 (article number; no page range in record)
papers.population_and_n: Case-control study of Ugandan children with P. falciparum malaria: 87 total (29 uncomplicated, 27 severe malarial anaemia, 31 cerebral malaria); 58 severe cases in outcome analysis (19 fatal, 39 non-fatal); plus mouse experiments (group sizes not in abstract).
papers.abstract_summary: The authors measured the haem-haemopexin axis in 87 Ugandan children with falciparum malaria. Haemin was higher and haemopexin lower in both severe malarial anaemia and cerebral malaria than in uncomplicated malaria (haemin p<0.01; haemopexin p<0.0001). Among the 58 severe cases, higher haemin and cell-free haemoglobin at presentation were associated with death (p<0.05). In mice, cerebral-malaria-susceptible C57BL/6 animals had lower circulating haemopexin than resistant BALB/c animals (p<0.01), and haemopexin-gene-deleted mice had higher mortality than wild-type littermates (p<0.05). The work links depletion of the haem scavenger haemopexin and rising free haem to severe disease and death. (Paraphrased from the PubMed record as returned by WebFetch.)
papers.key_finding: Haemopexin was depleted and free haemin raised in severe malarial anaemia and cerebral malaria; haemin and cell-free Hb predicted death; Hpx-null mice died more.
papers.corrections: Published December 2015, i.e. just before the requested 2016-2026 window; included because it is the best human falciparum study of haemopexin depletion specifically. PubMed record (efetch XML) has no CommentsCorrectionsList entries. Abstract names haptoglobin among plasma measurements but reports no haptoglobin result. Case-control design in children, n modest, and a mouse component.

connections.shared_pathway: Immune-mediated (antibody-driven) erythrocyte destruction layered on parasite-driven haemolysis, with asplenia/splenectomy as a risk modifier
connections.canine_evidence: Canine babesiosis includes Coombs-positive haemolysis in a B. canis pup (CB096, n=1) and flow-cytometric IMHA/IMTP (Evans syndrome) in a smear-negative, PCR-positive B. canis dog that improved on antiparasitic plus immunosuppressive therapy (CB047, n=1). In 55 dogs with IMHA, concurrent PCR-confirmed B. gibsoni independently predicted death (CB153, HR 2.6, p=0.024), and secondary IMHA raised recurrence risk in B. gibsoni (CB067, n=145). Splenectomised dogs developed severe or life-threatening anaemia with B. vogeli (CB021, n=6) and marrow haemophagocytic syndrome with B. vulpes (CB132, n=1, immunosuppression plus antiprotozoals). A narrative review argues canine babesial anaemia is largely host-immune driven (CB107). Regenerative response is inadequate in B. rossi (CB115).
connections.human_evidence: PMID 28273010: in 86 babesiosis patients, 6 (all asplenic, P<0.001) developed warm AIHA 2-4 weeks after diagnosis, after clinical response and parasitaemia clearance; all had DAT positive for IgG and C3 with warm autoantibodies; 4 of 6 needed immunosuppression. Supporting only (not selected papers): case reports and a literature review (PMID 34007364, PMID 40790611) report the same pattern of IgG-positive DAT, asplenia and steroid response.
connections.differences: Human data are from B. microti in a US hospital cohort, with the key phenomenon being post-clearance autoimmune haemolysis in asplenic patients; canine evidence is almost entirely single-case reports (CB047, CB096) or IMHA cohorts where Babesia is a co-factor rather than the cause (CB153, CB067), mostly B. canis/gibsoni/vogeli/rossi in intact dogs. Complement (C3) coating, the post-clearance timing and the autoantibody specificity have not been shown in dogs in the digest. Canine IMHA labelling relies on Coombs/spherocytosis/flow cytometry, with less standardised criteria; whether antibody is autoantibody or parasite-antigen-adsorbed is unresolved in both hosts. Dog spleen status was explicit only in the experimental/case-report splenectomy studies.
connections.strength_rationale: Antibody-mediated red cell destruction in the setting of Babesia infection has been documented in both hosts (DAT/Coombs-positive haemolysis, response to immunosuppression), and asplenia worsens disease in both. But the canine documentation is two n=1 case reports plus co-factor cohorts, and the human defining feature (post-clearance WAHA with IgG+C3 DAT, n=6 of 86) has no canine cohort counterpart, so it is not 'directly demonstrated in both'.

connections.shared_pathway: Intravascular haemolysis releasing cell-free haemoglobin and free haem, depleting scavengers (haptoglobin, haemopexin), with oxidative injury to kidney and other organs
connections.canine_evidence: The specific axis (cell-free Hb, free haem, haptoglobin, haemopexin) was not measured in any ERY or ERY (secondary) study in the digest. Indirect indicators of haemolysis and oxidative stress: hyperbilirubinaemia in 90% (CB099) and pigmenturia in 26% (CB149, from the digest's other sections as cited in the digest), haemolysis-related pathways in whole-blood RNA-seq of experimental B. rossi infection (CB082, n=5), lowered SOD/GPx/catalase with raised MDA tied to MODS and death (CB006), oxidative-stress changes in B. canis, B. gibsoni and B. vogeli (CB051, CB075, CB076, CB077, CB083), a review concluding oxidative erythrocyte injury contributes to haemolysis (CB114), and liver lesions attributed to haemolysis and hypoxia (CB147, n=10). One serum proteomics study found hemopexin more abundant in infected dogs (CB117, 3 vs 3 dogs), the opposite direction to the depletion seen in falciparum malaria and consistent with an acute-phase rise.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 28449641: in 107 adults with severe falciparum malaria, CFH correlated with haemolysis markers and parasite burden (PfHRP2) and with F2-isoprostanes; AKI (58%) patients had higher CFH (8.8 vs 5.1 microM), F2-isoprostanes and isofurans, and lipid-peroxidation markers predicted dialysis and death. PMID 26691827: in 87 Ugandan children, haemopexin was lower and haemin higher in severe malarial anaemia and cerebral malaria than uncomplicated malaria, and haemin and CFH predicted death among 58 severe cases; Hpx-null mice had higher mortality.
connections.differences: Falciparum malaria involves cytoadherent sequestration, PfHRP2-measured parasite burden, high-density parasitaemia and haem-induced endothelial and renal injury; much of the CFH burden is attributed to schizont rupture and, in the studies, a role for NO scavenging. B. canis, B. rossi and others differ in host-cell invasion, lack the same sequestration biology, and, to the knowledge of this review (not verified in the digest), do not form haemozoin, so haem handling may differ. Canine studies used oxidative markers (SOD, MDA) rather than haem or scavenger assays; antioxidant enzyme patterns in dogs are inconsistent in direction across studies (CB006 low versus CB077 raised erythrocyte SOD/CAT). Human malaria data are adult (Bangladesh) and paediatric (Uganda) cohorts with severe malaria, not equivalent to canine babesiosis; neither human paper is a babesiosis study, and no human babesiosis study of CFH/haptoglobin/haemopexin was found in the search.
connections.strength_rationale: Haemolysis and oxidative stress are shown in canine babesiosis, but the cell-free Hb/haem/haptoglobin/haemopexin axis itself has not been measured in dogs in the digest, and the single canine hemopexin finding (CB117, n=3 vs 3) points the opposite way. The human evidence is from falciparum malaria only, with no human babesiosis counterpart located, so the mechanism is inferred by analogy.

papers.title: Elevated plasma interleukin-8 as a risk factor for mortality in children presenting with cerebral malaria.
papers.population_and_n: Children with P. falciparum cerebral malaria, southern Benin; n=70 (50 survivors, 20 deaths); CSF multiplex PCR (14 pathogens) used to exclude co-infection; plasma Luminex (17 markers) and urinary assays (7 markers) at inclusion, D3 and D30
papers.abstract_summary: Seventy Beninese children with P. falciparum cerebral malaria were followed to outcome (50 survived, 20 died). Co-infections were excluded by multiplex PCR on cerebrospinal fluid. Seventeen plasma and seven urinary markers of inflammation and oxidative stress were measured on admission and at days 3 and 30. In univariate analysis, TNF, IL-1beta, IL-10, IL-8, CXCL9, granzyme B and angiopoietin-2 were higher, and urinary PGE2 metabolite lower, in children who died. In multivariable logistic models, high admission plasma IL-8 was the main independent risk factor for death (adjusted OR 14.2, P=0.002). Follow-up samples showed markers of resolution (CXCL5, CCL17, CCL22, urinary 15-F2t-isoprostane), and markers tied to neutrophil activation, endothelial activation and damage, and inflammatory/oxidative responses tracked aggravation.
papers.key_finding: In 70 children with cerebral malaria, TNF, IL-1beta, IL-8, IL-10 and CXCL9 were higher in the 20 who died; admission IL-8 was the strongest independent mortality predictor (aOR 14.2).
papers.corrections: None. PubMed CommentsCorrections list is empty (no erratum, retraction or expression of concern); publication type Journal Article.

papers.title: Activated Neutrophils Are Associated with Pediatric Cerebral Malaria Vasculopathy in Malawian Children.
papers.population_and_n: Malawian children with cerebral malaria (Blantyre Malaria Project); abstract gives no n. Per PMC full text: whole-blood transcriptomes from 97 children (64 malarial-retinopathy-positive Ret+CM, 33 retinopathy-negative Ret-CM); plasma neutrophil proteins in 51 Ret+CM vs 25 Ret-CM; autopsy brain samples examined
papers.abstract_summary: The authors compared peripheral whole-blood transcriptomes of Malawian children with cerebral malaria and retinopathy (a marker of cerebral sequestration of infected red cells, Ret+CM) against children with cerebral malaria without retinopathy (Ret-CM). Ret+CM showed upregulation of 103 gene-set pathways, including cytokine, coagulation and extracellular-matrix pathways, and neutrophil transcripts were the most strongly upregulated individual genes. Plasma neutrophil elastase, myeloperoxidase and proteinase 3 (but not lactoferrin or lipocalin) were higher in Ret+CM, while neutrophil chemotaxis was impaired, possibly linked to raised plasma heme. Neutrophils were rare in autopsy brain microvessels and no extracellular traps were seen, implying effects mediated by soluble neutrophil products. Ret-CM children had less inflammation, higher interferon-alpha and Toll-like receptor pathway upregulation.
papers.key_finding: In Malawian children with cerebral malaria, neutrophil transcripts and plasma elastase, MPO and proteinase 3 were higher in those with retinopathy (cerebral sequestration), indicating neutrophil activation linked to severe vasculopathy.
papers.corrections: None. PubMed CommentsCorrections list is empty (no erratum or retraction). Note: abstract omits sample sizes; the n values above come from the PMC full text, not the abstract. Comparison is between two severe-malaria phenotypes, not severe versus uncomplicated; no uncomplicated-malaria or healthy control comparison in the abstract.

papers.title: Whole blood transcriptomics reveals sepsis mortality-associated changes in neutrophil degranulation.
papers.journal: American Journal of Respiratory Cell and Molecular Biology
papers.population_and_n: Critically ill adults with sepsis, prospective observational cohort, University of Pennsylvania; n=161 (60 died within 30 days, 37%); independent validation cohort n=479 with 28-day mortality
papers.abstract_summary: In a prospective cohort of 161 critically ill sepsis patients, whole-blood RNA was collected within 24 hours of ICU admission and profiled by microarray. Gene expression in 30-day non-survivors was compared with survivors, adjusting for age, sex and neutrophil count. There were 1106 differentially expressed genes in non-survivors, including neutrophil granule genes (CEACAM8, ELANE, PRTN3, MPO, CEACAM6, DEFA4, MS4A3) expressed more than 1.8-fold higher despite the neutrophil-count adjustment. The neutrophil degranulation pathway was over-represented in differentially expressed genes in both the discovery and an independent 479-patient cohort, by gene set enrichment, and in four of six co-expression modules correlated with mortality. The authors conclude that neutrophil degranulation genes are involved in sepsis mortality and may be a modifiable target.
papers.key_finding: In 161 ICU sepsis patients, neutrophil granule genes (MPO, ELANE, PRTN3, DEFA4) were over-expressed in 30-day non-survivors independent of neutrophil count, replicated in 479 patients.
papers.corrections: None. PubMed CommentsCorrections list is empty (no erratum or retraction). Publication type Journal Article; Observational Study. Transcript-level (microarray) evidence only; no protein or functional neutrophil assay in the abstract.

connections.shared_pathway: Circulating pro-inflammatory cytokine/chemokine response (TNF, IL-8/CXCL8-family, IL-1beta, IL-6, MCP-1) scaling with disease severity and death: dysregulated innate cytokine response in an intra-erythrocytic parasitaemia
connections.canine_evidence: CB037 (B. rossi, n=55 PCR-positive dogs plus 17 controls): IL-6, MCP-1 and TNF-alpha rose with severity and were higher in the 9 non-survivors, while IL-8 fell with severity. CB017 (B. canis, n=31 infected, 16 healthy): day-1 MCP-1 and KC-like (the canine CXCL1/IL-8 functional homologue) were higher in complicated dogs (MCP-1 AUC 0.906); IL-8 correlated inversely with RBC and haematocrit in uncomplicated dogs. CB098/CB101 (experimental B. rossi, 5 infected Beagles): inflammation (cytokines, CRP) began before clinical disease, was dose-dependent, and treatment transiently amplified cytokine and CRP responses; CB082 (same model) whole-blood RNA-seq showed innate and interferon pathway activation. CB109 (B. canis, n=32 babesiosis in gene-expression subset): highest IFN-gamma and SOCS3 expression in severe disease. CB107 narrative review argues cytokines drive the anaemia. All natural-infection data are associational and single-centre.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 36759905 (Royo 2023; n=70 paediatric cerebral malaria, 20 deaths): TNF, IL-1beta, IL-8, IL-10, CXCL9, granzyme B and angiopoietin-2 higher in those who died; admission IL-8 independent mortality risk factor (aOR 14.2). Supporting context for severe-malaria generally (not among the three selected papers, not independently verified here): PMID 35467747 (TNF), 35396564 (IL-6) and 39567619 (MCP-1/CCL2) are systematic reviews reporting higher levels in severe than non-severe malaria, but with I2 above 97%. No primary human babesiosis study measuring cytokine levels against severity was found in PubMed (see search_log); the only human babesiosis host-response severity signal found was falling LDL/HDL in admitted patients (PMID 37111499, n=39 retrospective), which is an acute-phase/lipoprotein finding rather than a cytokine finding.
connections.differences: 1) The canine and human cohorts used different outcomes: dogs were classified by 'complicated' (organ dysfunction) or survival, children by cerebral malaria death. 2) IL-8 is discordant: low IL-8 tracked severity in B. rossi dogs (CB037) but high IL-8 predicted death in children (Royo); dogs' KC-like in CB017 was higher in complicated cases, so canine IL-8/KC data themselves conflict, and assay platforms and canine cross-reactivity differ. 3) P. falciparum infected red cells cytoadhere and sequester in the brain microvasculature, whereas Babesia sequestration in dogs is only proposed (CB041) and cerebral babesiosis is rare. 4) Host age, splenic status, co-infection control (Royo excluded co-infection; many canine cohorts did not), and treatment timing differ; CB098 shows treatment itself alters cytokine kinetics. 5) Mortality is small in the canine series (9 non-survivors in CB037) and 20 in Royo, so both estimates are imprecise. 6) Neither dataset shows causation; a cytokine storm as such has not been defined or demonstrated in canine babesiosis. 7) Human babesiosis is the closer parasite comparator, but no equivalent primary cytokine-severity data exist.
connections.strength_rationale: Same measured variable (elevated circulating TNF and chemokines in natural-infection non-survivors or severe cases vs milder cases) is reported in dogs (CB037, CB017) and humans (PMID 36759905). Rated at the level of an association, not a causal cytokine-storm mechanism. IL-8 direction is contradictory, and the human data come from malaria, not babesiosis, so confidence in cross-species transfer is moderate.

connections.shared_pathway: Neutrophil activation and degranulation (myeloperoxidase, elastase, proteinase 3 granule proteins) associated with severe disease and death
connections.canine_evidence: CB050 (B. rossi, retrospective analysis of two cohorts, n=140 infected, 20 controls): mean peroxidase index of neutrophils (MPXI) was higher in infected dogs (P=0.033) and highest in non-survivors (P=0.011) than controls, and correlated with pro-inflammatory cytokines in non-survivors; mortality 11%. CB073 (B. canis, n=54): leukopenia and monocytopenia, not parasite load or acute-phase proteins, were independent correlates of SIRS. CB082 (experimental B. rossi, n=5): whole-blood RNA-seq showed innate immune pathway activation. CB054 and CB111 (necropsy series) show macrophage expansion in spleen and increased macrophages/T cells in lung; no canine study measured neutrophil elastase, MPO protein release, degranulation transcripts or NETs directly. MPXI is a haematology-analyser readout of peroxidase staining intensity whose link to activation or degranulation is inferred.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 26884431 (Feintuch 2016; Malawian children with cerebral malaria): neutrophil transcripts were the most upregulated genes in retinopathy-positive (cerebral sequestration) disease; plasma neutrophil elastase, MPO and proteinase 3 were higher (n=51 vs 25 per full text), neutrophil chemotaxis impaired, no NETs in autopsy brain. PMID 41738283 (Giannini 2026; sepsis, n=161 plus 479 validation): MPO, ELANE, PRTN3, DEFA4 and CEACAM8 transcripts were more than 1.8-fold higher in 30-day non-survivors after adjustment for neutrophil count, and the neutrophil degranulation pathway was replicated in the second cohort. PMID 42029096 (2026) reports that B. microti vesicles trigger NETosis and cytokine release in mouse neutrophils in vitro; this is murine, in vitro, and was not used as a human comparator.
connections.differences: 1) Readouts differ: canine MPXI (cytochemical index from an analyser) versus human granule-gene transcripts (sepsis) and plasma granule proteins (malaria); the canine measure does not distinguish activation from degranulation or from increased granulocyte maturity. 2) Feintuch compares two severe malaria phenotypes, so the neutrophil signal marks cerebral sequestration vasculopathy, not death or severity versus mild disease; sequestration biology is specific to P. falciparum. 3) Sepsis is mostly bacterial and adult, with ICU treatment, vasopressors and organ support; canine cohorts are untreated or recently treated infections with different baseline neutrophil biology. 4) Canine cohorts (CB050) include no mechanistic neutrophil assays, and no study shows a neutrophil-driven pathway in canine babesiosis or in human babesiosis (neutropenia is described in human babesiosis, PMID 26071466, but not mechanistically). 5) Giannini adjusted for neutrophil count; CB050 did not adjust for count or maturity.
connections.strength_rationale: Both hosts show a neutrophil-activation signal linked to worse outcome, but through non-equivalent measurements (MPXI in dogs; granule transcripts and plasma proteins in humans) and in different diseases; no neutrophil granule protein, NET or degranulation measure exists in dogs or in human babesiosis, so the pathway is plausible rather than shown in both.

connections.shared_pathway: Interferon/regulatory counter-response (IFN-gamma, SOCS3, IL-10, type I interferon) balancing or failing to restrain inflammation in severe disease
connections.canine_evidence: CB109 (B. canis, n=32 babesiosis in gene-expression subset with 3 healthy controls): highest IFN-gamma and SOCS3 expression in severe babesiosis. CB082 (experimental B. rossi, n=5): interferon/antiviral pathway responses in whole-blood RNA-seq. CB075 (B. vogeli, subgroups of about 4-5 dogs): higher IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha than healthy dogs. CB008 (B. rossi, n=44): complicated cases had lower CD3+ and CD4+ percentages, read as immune suppression. No canine IL-10 or type I interferon severity data appear in the INF digest.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 36759905: IL-10 (anti-inflammatory), CXCL9 (IFN-gamma-induced) and granzyme B were higher in fatal paediatric cerebral malaria, consistent with an IFN-gamma axis accompanied by a compensatory regulatory signal. PMID 26884431: Ret-CM children (no cerebral sequestration) had lower inflammation, higher alpha interferon and Toll-like receptor pathway upregulation than Ret+CM.
connections.differences: Canine IFN-gamma/SOCS3 data are tiny and mRNA-based (CB109) or from very small groups (CB075); human data are plasma proteins and transcriptomes; cause and effect are unknown in both; the human interferon-alpha signal is linked to absence of sequestration in malaria, a feature not shown for Babesia. Co-infections (E. canis in CB075) are a confounder in the canine data.
connections.strength_rationale: Both hosts show interferon-axis and regulatory-cytokine changes in severe disease, but the canine evidence is small, partly mRNA-only, and not paired with an IL-10 or interferon-alpha comparison, and direction relative to protection versus pathology is unresolved.

papers.title: Severe babesiosis in Long Island: review of 34 cases and their complications.
papers.study_type: human case series (foundational, older; labelled as such because no recent primary human babesiosis study measuring coagulation was found)
papers.population_and_n: 34 consecutive hospitalised adults with severe Babesia infection over 13 years (Long Island, New York, USA), compared with uninfected febrile control patients (control n not given in abstract); 7 had exchange transfusion, 3 died.
papers.abstract_summary: Over 13 years the authors identified 34 consecutive hospitalised patients with severe babesiosis and compared them with uninfected febrile controls. Cases more often had malaise, arthralgia, myalgia and dyspnoea, and more often had thrombocytopenia and abnormal liver function. Forty-one percent developed complications including acute respiratory failure, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), congestive heart failure and renal failure. Complicated disease was associated with severe anaemia (haemoglobin below 10 g/dL, P=.01) and higher parasitaemia (above 10%, P=.08). Treatment combined clindamycin, quinine, atovaquone or azithromycin; parasitaemia persisted a mean of 8.5 days (range 3-21). Exchange transfusion lowered high parasitaemia in 7 patients. Three patients died. The abstract gives no breakdown of how many patients had DIC and no laboratory coagulation measurements.
papers.key_finding: In 34 severe human babesiosis cases, thrombocytopenia was commoner than in febrile controls and 41% had complications including DIC; complicated disease tracked severe anaemia and high parasitaemia.
papers.corrections: PubMed record checked 2026-10-23: no CommentsCorrections entries, no erratum, no retraction notice.

papers.title: A Novel Assay for Neutrophil Extracellular Trap Formation Independently Predicts Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation and Mortality in Critically Ill Patients.
papers.journal: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
papers.study_type: primary human cohort (prospective, sepsis-predominant ICU population; sepsis comparator, not babesiosis)
papers.population_and_n: 341 consecutive adult ICU patients (UK); strong NET formation found predominantly in sepsis. Sepsis subgroup size not given in abstract.
papers.abstract_summary: The authors built an ex vivo assay in which patient plasma from ICU admission is incubated with isolated neutrophils to semiquantify NET-forming capacity. Among 341 consecutive adult ICU patients, NET formation was absent in 22.0%, mild in 49.9%, moderate in 14.4% and strong in 13.8%, with strong formation mostly in sepsis. After adjustment for APACHE II, the degree of NET formation independently predicted DIC and 28-day mortality, whereas cell-free DNA, myeloperoxidase and myeloperoxidase-DNA complexes did not. IL-8 concentration was strongly associated with NET formation, blocking IL-8 attenuated NETosis, and MAPK activation by IL-8 was identified as a major pathway. The assay measures NET-inducing capacity of plasma rather than circulating NETs.
papers.key_finding: In 341 ICU patients, plasma NET-forming capacity independently predicted DIC and 28-day mortality after APACHE II adjustment; strong NET formation was mainly in sepsis.
papers.corrections: PubMed record checked 2026-10-23: no erratum or retraction. One CommentIn entry (editorial: Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019;200(7):798-799, PMID 31185179), which is commentary, not a correction.

papers.title: Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria is associated with circulating ultra-large von Willebrand multimers and ADAMTS13 inhibition.
papers.study_type: primary human cohort (prospective, patients vs controls; foundational, older; labelled as such because more recent human work on ADAMTS13 in malaria is weaker or limited to case reports, meta-analysis and review)
papers.population_and_n: Ghanaian patients with severe P. falciparum malaria (n=20) and cerebral malaria (n=13), plus controls (control n not given in abstract).
papers.abstract_summary: This prospective Ghanaian study of severe (n=20) and cerebral (n=13) falciparum malaria tested whether raised von Willebrand factor (VWF) reflects a functional change. Plasma VWF antigen was raised, and VWF collagen-binding activity was disproportionately raised (medians 7.6 and 7.0 IU/ml in cerebral and severe malaria versus 1.9 IU/ml in controls, p<0.005), correlating with abnormal ultra-large VWF multimers. ADAMTS13 activity was persistently reduced to about 55% of normal (p<0.005). Mixing studies with patient plasma and pooled normal plasma plus recombinant ADAMTS13 showed time-dependent inhibition of ADAMTS13 function. This was not explained by known inhibitors (IL-6, free haemoglobin, factor VIII, thrombospondin-1), so an unidentified inhibitor was suggested.
papers.key_finding: In severe and cerebral falciparum malaria, VWF collagen-binding and ultra-large multimers were raised while ADAMTS13 activity fell to about 55% of normal, with functional inhibition in plasma-mixing studies.
papers.corrections: PubMed record checked 2026-10-23: no CommentsCorrections entries, no erratum, no retraction notice.

connections.shared_pathway: Consumptive coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia progressing to DIC in severe haemoprotozoal infection (platelet consumption, antithrombin loss, fibrinolytic shutdown, microthrombi)
connections.canine_evidence: CB145 (B. rossi, 97 dogs vs 15 controls, 12 non-survivors with necropsy): severe thrombocytopenia, platelet activation, factor consumption, fibrinolytic shutdown and fibrin microthrombi with high CRP/SAA, i.e. a thromboinflammatory phenotype. CB011 (B. canis, n=25): antithrombin III decreased and TAT raised. CB034 (B. rossi, n=13): higher fibrinogen and fibrin clot strength offsetting low platelets on thromboelastography. CB079 (B. gibsoni, n=1) and CB005 (captive wolf) report DIC. Thrombocytopenia is near-universal across CB022, CB048, CB056, CB064, CB078, CB131.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 11283800 (Hatcher 2001, n=34 severe human babesiosis): thrombocytopenia more frequent than in febrile controls, and 41% had complications including DIC, associated with severe anaemia and parasitaemia above 10% (borderline). PMID 31162936 is a sepsis comparator, not babesiosis. No coagulation assay data in human babesiosis were found in the retrieved literature, and recent human babesiosis hits were case reports (e.g. splenic infarction, thrombocytopenia, DIC with HLH) or administrative cohorts such as PMID 41666444 (TriNetX babesiosis sepsis, n=1,566, ICD-code based).
connections.differences: The canine data measure mechanism (TAT, antithrombin, fibrinolysis, TEG, necropsy microthrombi). The human babesiosis data are clinical counts only, with no mechanism and no DIC definition in the abstract. Different species: B. rossi, B. canis and B. gibsoni versus mainly B. microti in the US (Hatcher; species not stated in abstract). The human series is from severe, hospitalised, often asplenic or older patients, whereas the canine cohorts include uncomplicated cases. Treatment and supportive care differ. B. rossi dogs show hyperfibrinogenaemia and fibrinolytic shutdown that has not been tested in humans.
connections.strength_rationale: Thrombocytopenia and DIC occur clinically in both hosts, but only the canine studies measure the consumptive and fibrinolytic mechanism. Human babesiosis lacks the same measurements, so overlap rests on clinical syndrome plus the shared biology of severe haemolytic parasitaemia.

connections.shared_pathway: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) as a driver of immunothrombosis and DIC
connections.canine_evidence: No NET, citrullinated histone or cell-free DNA measurement appears in the COA or COA (secondary) digest entries. The nearest canine data are CB145 (thromboinflammation: platelet activation, fibrin microthrombi, high CRP/SAA, 97 dogs) and CB004 (HMGB-1 raised in 30 B. canis dogs, a damage-associated molecular pattern that can induce NETs, but NETs were not measured). CB078 notes neutrophils low or normal in large Babesia infections.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 31162936 (Abrams 2019, 341 ICU patients, mostly sepsis for strong NET responders): plasma NET-forming capacity independently predicted DIC and 28-day mortality after APACHE II adjustment, and IL-8 was a driver. This is sepsis, not babesiosis. A malaria NET cohort (PMID 30452670, Kho 2019, severe falciparum n=8) found NETs rising with severity but its severe group is very small and the record carries an erratum (PMID 30768162, content not inspected). No human babesiosis NET study was found.
connections.differences: NETs were not measured in canine or human babesiosis in the retrieved material, so the link is carried entirely by sepsis. Abrams measures plasma NET-inducing capacity ex vivo, not circulating NETs in tissue. Sepsis is bacteria-driven and IL-8 dependent; babesiosis is intraerythrocytic with haemolysis and free haem, which can also trigger NETs in malaria models but is untested here. Dog neutrophil NET biology (canine NETs exist in vitro) has not been linked to babesiosis outcomes in the digest.
connections.strength_rationale: No study in either host measures NETs in babesiosis. The connection is an inference from sepsis-DIC data and from thromboinflammation markers (CB145, CB004) that do not specifically implicate NETs.

connections.shared_pathway: Endothelial activation with microvascular thrombosis and dysregulation of the VWF-ADAMTS13 axis in severe haemoprotozoal disease
connections.canine_evidence: CB004 (B. canis, 30 dogs vs 10 controls; 11 complicated): thrombomodulin, VCAM-1, HMGB-1 and suPAR raised, indicating endothelial activation and altered fibrinolysis, shifting or normalising by day 6. CB145: fibrin microthrombi at necropsy in non-survivors. CB041 (narrative review): proposed capillary sequestration of infected erythrocytes via endothelial attachment, consolidated by coagulation. VWF and ADAMTS13 were not measured in any COA digest entry.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 19300493 (Larkin 2009, severe n=20, cerebral n=13 falciparum): raised VWF antigen, disproportionately raised VWF collagen-binding, abnormal ultra-large multimers, ADAMTS13 activity about 55% of normal and plasma inhibition of ADAMTS13. Supporting context seen but not selected: PMID 26830467 (Ugandan children, VWF antigen associated with mortality) and PMID 40283058 (2025 meta-analysis: VWF higher in malaria than controls, SMD 2.689, 12 studies, 3,109 participants, but no significant severe versus non-severe difference, I2 above 98%).
connections.differences: Different markers: canine studies measured thrombomodulin, VCAM-1, suPAR, whereas the human data measured VWF and ADAMTS13; endothelial activation is shared but the specific VWF-ADAMTS13 mechanism is not shown in dogs. P. falciparum sequesters via PfEMP1 binding to ICAM-1 and EPCR in brain and organ microvasculature; sequestration in B. canis is only proposed (CB041) and not shown to depend on a comparable adhesin. Larkin is a single-timepoint Ghanaian study with an unidentified inhibitor; the 2025 meta-analysis shows heterogeneous severity effects. Splenic status matters: CB021 shows B. vogeli is severe mainly in splenectomised dogs, a host factor that also shapes human babesiosis.
connections.strength_rationale: Endothelial activation with microthrombosis is demonstrated in canine babesiosis (CB004, CB145) and in severe malaria (Larkin), but the VWF-ADAMTS13 imbalance itself has been measured only in malaria. Biological plausibility is supported but not demonstrated in babesiosis.

papers.title: Intravascular haemolysis in severe Plasmodium knowlesi malaria: association with endothelial activation, microvascular dysfunction, and acute kidney injury.
papers.population_and_n: Hospitalised Malaysian adults with P. knowlesi malaria: 48 severe, 154 non-severe, 50 healthy controls
papers.abstract_summary: The authors studied hospitalised adults with knowlesi malaria and healthy controls. They measured cell-free haemoglobin as a marker of intravascular haemolysis. They also measured the endothelial markers angiopoietin-2 and osteoprotegerin, plus ICAM-1, E-selectin, IL-6, creatinine and lactate. Microvascular reactivity and nitric oxide-dependent endothelial function were assessed as well. Cell-free haemoglobin rose with disease severity and tracked parasitaemia. It was higher than in severe falciparum malaria from the same research group. Cell-free haemoglobin was also linked to angiopoietin-2 and osteoprotegerin. Osteoprotegerin was independently associated with the adhesion molecules, impaired microvascular reactivity and nitric oxide-dependent endothelial dysfunction. Acute kidney injury occurred in 88% of severe cases, and both angiopoietin-2 and osteoprotegerin were independent risk factors for it. The authors propose that haemolysis-driven endothelial activation contributes to end-organ injury. The abstract does not report effect sizes.
papers.key_finding: In severe knowlesi malaria, haemolysis tracked Ang-2 and osteoprotegerin, impaired microvascular and NO-dependent function, and independent risk of AKI (88% of severe cases).
papers.corrections: PubMed XML shows no CommentsCorrections elements (no erratum, retraction or expression of concern).

papers.title: Glycocalyx Breakdown Is Associated With Severe Disease and Fatal Outcome in Plasmodium falciparum Malaria.
papers.population_and_n: Adult inpatients in Indonesia with falciparum malaria: 43 severe, 57 moderately severe, 29 healthy controls (n=129); 3 deaths among severe cases
papers.abstract_summary: This prospective study asked whether breakdown of the endothelial glycocalyx tracks with severity and death in adult falciparum malaria. Urinary glycosaminoglycans were measured by dye-binding assay and by mass spectrometry, and normalised to creatinine. Levels were highest in severe disease (dye assay mean 3.98; mass spectrometry 6.82), intermediate in moderately severe disease (1.78; 4.87) and lowest in controls (0.22; 1.24), with P below 0.001. Within the severe group, the 3 patients who died had higher levels than the 39 survivors (medians 6.72 vs 3.10 by dye assay and 12.15 vs 4.64 by mass spectrometry; P=0.03). Glycocalyx breakdown correlated with parasite biomass and was inversely related to endothelial nitric oxide bioavailability. The authors conclude that glycocalyx degradation is linked to severe disease and fatal outcome.
papers.key_finding: Urinary glycosaminoglycan (glycocalyx breakdown) rose with falciparum severity, was higher in the 3 deaths than 39 survivors, and was inversely linked to endothelial NO bioavailability.
papers.corrections: No erratum, retraction or expression of concern. PubMed lists one CommentIn (editorial: Clin Infect Dis 2019;69(10):1721-1723, PMID 30698670). Mortality comparison rests on only 3 deaths.

papers.title: Angiopoietin-2 outperforms other endothelial biomarkers associated with severe acute kidney injury in patients with severe sepsis and respiratory failure.
papers.population_and_n: 228 adults with severe sepsis and acute respiratory failure (VALID prospective cohort); 141 developed KDIGO stage 2-3 AKI
papers.abstract_summary: This prospective observational study used the VALID cohort of adults with severe sepsis and acute respiratory failure. Of 228 patients, 141 developed severe acute kidney injury (KDIGO stage 2 or 3). Four plasma endothelial markers were measured at enrolment: angiopoietin-2, soluble VE-cadherin, endocan and syndecan-1. All four were higher in patients with severe AKI, but only angiopoietin-2 stayed independently associated with it (odds ratio 6.07 per log increase, 95% CI 2.34-15.78, p<0.001). Angiopoietin-2 also rose with hepatic, coagulation and circulatory organ failure, and was higher in non-pulmonary than pulmonary sepsis. The authors conclude that early endothelial injury, best captured by angiopoietin-2, is linked to sepsis-associated AKI and wider organ dysfunction.
papers.key_finding: In 228 septic patients with respiratory failure, only Ang-2 (not syndecan-1, endocan or sVE-cadherin) independently predicted severe AKI (OR 6.07 per log increase).
papers.corrections: PubMed XML shows no CommentsCorrections elements (no erratum, retraction or expression of concern).

connections.shared_pathway: Systemic endothelial activation shown by soluble endothelial markers (adhesion molecules, thrombomodulin) that rise with infection and relate to organ dysfunction
connections.canine_evidence: CB004 (2017, B. canis, n=30 infected dogs, 11 complicated and 19 uncomplicated, vs 10 healthy controls): thrombomodulin, HMGB-1, VCAM-1 and suPAR were raised versus healthy dogs and normalised or shifted by day 6. CB145 (2026, B. rossi, n=97 infected, 12 non-survivors, 15 controls): thromboinflammation with platelet activation, fibrinolytic shutdown and fibrin microthrombi at necropsy. CB087 (2021, n=187 dogs): endothelial desquamation in spleens (descriptive).
connections.human_evidence: PMID 29872039: ICAM-1, E-selectin, Ang-2 and osteoprotegerin rose with severity in P. knowlesi malaria (48 severe, 154 non-severe, 50 controls), and osteoprotegerin was independently linked to ICAM-1 and E-selectin. PMID 33541396: Ang-2, sVE-cadherin, endocan and syndecan-1 were all higher in septic patients with severe AKI (n=228).
connections.differences: The analytes overlap only at the class level (VCAM-1 and thrombomodulin in dogs; ICAM-1, E-selectin and Ang-2 in humans). The canine cohorts are small, with 10-15 controls, and CB004 and CB145 are associational. Dogs were sampled at admission with variable treatment and the digest does not show a marker-to-outcome link in CB004. Human assays are validated for human proteins and canine cross-reactivity is a separate issue. Sepsis has no parasite, and P. knowlesi is not a sequestering parasite to the degree P. falciparum is.
connections.strength_rationale: Endothelial activation by soluble markers was measured in both hosts (CB004 in B. canis; PMIDs 29872039 and 33541396 in humans). The claim is limited to the generic phenomenon, because the specific markers differ and the dog data are associational. It does not extend to the Ang-2/Tie2 axis.

connections.shared_pathway: Angiopoietin-2 release and Tie2 destabilisation of the endothelium, with Ang-2 as an independent predictor of organ injury (AKI)
connections.canine_evidence: No canine study in the END digest measured angiopoietin-2, angiopoietin-1 or Tie2. The closest data are CB004 (thrombomodulin, VCAM-1 and HMGB-1 raised, n=30 vs 10 controls), CB122 (serum extracellular vesicle proteins from B. canis dogs enriched for adhesion and VEGF pathways, preliminary, 15 vs 15), and CB145 (thromboinflammation, 97 dogs).
connections.human_evidence: PMID 29872039: Ang-2 rose with severity in P. knowlesi malaria and was an independent risk factor for AKI (AKI in 88% of severe cases). PMID 33541396: Ang-2 was the only endothelial marker independently associated with severe AKI in sepsis (OR 6.07 per log increase, 95% CI 2.34-15.78). PMID 30753363: glycocalyx breakdown in falciparum malaria correlated with parasite biomass.
connections.differences: Ang-2 has not been measured in canine babesiosis, and a validated canine Ang-2 assay would be needed. Ang-2 is a non-specific marker of critical illness and also rises in non-infectious conditions, so rising Ang-2 in dogs would not by itself indicate a shared mechanism. Canine babesiosis AKI patterns differ (CB044 describes azotaemic and non-azotaemic dogs, hypotension and SIADH-like changes, not an endothelial AKI model).
connections.strength_rationale: Endothelial activation is demonstrated in dogs (CB004), and Ang-2 is a Weibel-Palade-body product and a generic downstream marker in human malaria and sepsis. However, no canine Ang-2 or Tie2 data exist in the digest, so the same mechanism has not been measured in both hosts.

connections.shared_pathway: Endothelial glycocalyx degradation (syndecan-1 shedding, urinary glycosaminoglycans) with vascular leak and organ dysfunction
connections.canine_evidence: No canine study in the END digest measured syndecan-1, heparan sulfate, urinary GAGs or glycocalyx imaging. Indirect, non-specific findings only: CB080 (2021, n=6 fatal B. canis) multi-organ congestion, oedema, effusions and proposed circulatory failure; CB146 (2026) cardiac haemorrhage, oedema, congestion and effusion; CB111 (2023, B. rossi) alveolar oedema with exudative diffuse alveolar damage overlap; CB087 endothelial desquamation in the spleen.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 30753363: urinary GAGs were highest in severe falciparum malaria (n=129; dye assay mean 3.98 severe vs 0.22 controls), higher in 3 deaths than 39 survivors, and inversely related to NO bioavailability. PMID 33541396: syndecan-1 was higher in septic patients with severe AKI but was not independent of Ang-2 (n=228).
connections.differences: Oedema, effusions and congestion in dogs have many causes (hypoxia, hypoalbuminaemia, anaemia, inflammation, DIC) and the digest contains no glycocalyx-specific measurement. Syndecan-1 shedding in sepsis is heavily confounded by shock and fluid resuscitation. The human malaria data come from adults in endemic settings with different parasite biology.
connections.strength_rationale: Only non-specific pathology (oedema, congestion, endothelial desquamation) links the hosts. Glycocalyx degradation was measured in humans (PMID 30753363) but not in dogs in the digest, and shared clinical or histological signs alone are insufficient.

connections.shared_pathway: Haemolysis-driven loss of nitric oxide bioavailability (cell-free haemoglobin) causing endothelial dysfunction and impaired microvascular reactivity
connections.canine_evidence: No canine study in the END digest measured nitric oxide, ADMA, cell-free haemoglobin or flow-mediated vascular reactivity. Haemolytic anaemia is a hallmark of canine babesiosis across the digest (e.g. CB099: 82% anaemic and 90% hyperbilirubinaemic of 81 PCR-positive dogs). CB107 (review) attributes canine babesial anaemia mainly to host immune responses, and CB006 reports oxidative imbalance (lower SOD, GPx, catalase; higher MDA) associated with MODS and death in 40 dogs.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 29872039: cell-free haemoglobin rose with severity in P. knowlesi malaria and was linked to Ang-2 and osteoprotegerin, and osteoprotegerin was independently associated with impaired nitric oxide-dependent endothelial function and microvascular reactivity. PMID 30753363: glycocalyx breakdown was inversely linked to endothelial NO bioavailability in falciparum malaria.
connections.differences: Intravascular versus extravascular haemolysis proportions differ by Babesia species and by host, and splenic clearance matters (CB021: splenectomised B. vogeli dogs become severely anaemic and thrombocytopenic). NO bioavailability was measured functionally in humans (reactive hyperaemia-type testing) and has no canine equivalent in the digest. Oxidative-stress data in dogs (CB006) are not NO-specific.
connections.strength_rationale: Haemolysis is common to both diseases but the NO-scavenging step was measured only in human malaria (PMIDs 29872039 and 30753363). The dog evidence is limited to anaemia and generic oxidative stress markers, which are shared clinical signs rather than the same mechanism.

connections.shared_pathway: Microvascular obstruction and dysfunction (parasitised-cell sequestration, thromboinflammation, impaired microvascular reactivity) leading to hypoperfusion and organ failure
connections.canine_evidence: CB041 (2019, review of the author's own experimental B. canis model): proposes capillary sequestration of infected erythrocytes via endothelial attachment, consolidated by coagulation-mediated trapping, to explain severe disease despite low circulating parasitaemia. CB010 (2017): predicted B. canis exportome includes 103 VESA models (candidate cytoadhesion ligands; not functionally demonstrated here). CB145: fibrin microthrombi at necropsy in 12 non-survivors. CB080 (n=6) and CB146: congestion, haemorrhage, leukostasis and proposed circulatory failure. No in vivo canine microcirculation imaging is in the digest.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 29872039: impaired microvascular reactivity in severe knowlesi malaria, associated with endothelial activation and AKI. PMID 30753363: glycocalyx degradation tied to parasite biomass, severity and death in falciparum malaria. PMID 33541396: endothelial injury (Ang-2) linked to circulatory and coagulation organ failure in sepsis.
connections.differences: P. falciparum sequestration is mediated by PfEMP1 and is well characterised, whereas Babesia sequestration in dogs rests largely on one research group's model and a narrative review (CB041), and has not been shown by in vivo imaging. Knowlesi malaria shows severe disease with limited sequestration, so its microvascular dysfunction may be haemolysis and inflammation driven, which is the closer analogy to canine disease. Sepsis microcirculatory failure is not parasite-driven. Canine necropsy findings are end-stage and cannot show temporal sequence.
connections.strength_rationale: Canine histology (microthrombi, congestion, leukostasis) and the sequestration hypothesis are consistent with human microvascular dysfunction, but microcirculatory function itself was measured only in humans (PMID 29872039). The canine side is hypothesis and necropsy, not a direct measurement of the same variable.

papers.title: Cell-free hemoglobin mediated oxidative stress is associated with acute kidney injury and renal replacement therapy in severe falciparum malaria: an observational study.
papers.population_and_n: Bangladeshi adults with severe falciparum malaria (n=107), uncomplicated malaria (n=80) and sepsis (n=28); AKI at enrolment in 62/107 severe malaria patients
papers.abstract_summary: Prospective observational study testing whether cell-free haemoglobin (CFH) and CFH-driven lipid peroxidation contribute to severe malaria-associated AKI. At enrolment, CFH, F2-isoprostanes, isofurans, red cell deformability and creatinine were measured in 107 severe malaria patients, 80 uncomplicated malaria patients and 28 sepsis patients. AKI (creatinine at least 1.5x expected baseline) was present in 58% (62/107) of the severe malaria group. Those with AKI had higher geometric mean CFH (8.8 vs 5.1 uM, P=0.018), F2-isoprostanes (56.7 vs 27.8 pg/ml, P<0.001) and isofurans (109.2 vs 41.7 pg/ml, P<0.001). CFH correlated with haemolysis markers, PfHRP2 (parasite burden) and F2-isoprostanes. In mixed-effects models, F2-isoprostanes, isofurans, PfHRP2, CFH and red cell rigidity were independently associated with rising creatinine over 72 h. Admission F2-isoprostanes, isofurans and deformability predicted subsequent haemodialysis. The authors conclude CFH-mediated oxidative stress plausibly contributes to renal tubular injury.
papers.key_finding: In 107 severe falciparum malaria patients, AKI (58%) was associated with higher cell-free haemoglobin and lipid-peroxidation markers, which independently tracked rising creatinine and later dialysis.
papers.corrections: PubMed record checked (efetch XML, 2026): no CommentsCorrections entries, so no erratum, retraction or expression of concern is listed. Publication types: Journal Article; Observational Study.

papers.title: Neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL) predicts the occurrence of malaria-induced acute kidney injury.
papers.population_and_n: 39 travellers with imported P. falciparum malaria (Rotterdam Malaria Cohort; 10 with severe malaria); 6 developed AKI (15%)
papers.abstract_summary: Pilot evaluation study of whether structural tubular injury markers (serum NGAL, urine NGAL and urine KIM-1) identify AKI earlier than serum creatinine in imported falciparum malaria. Thirty-nine patients from the Rotterdam Malaria Cohort with stored serum and urine from presentation were included, 10 of whom met criteria for severe malaria. Six (15%) developed AKI. Serum NGAL, urine NGAL and urine KIM-1 all had large areas under the ROC curve for predicting AKI. Urine NGAL performed best: AUROC 1.00 (95% CI 1.00-1.00), PPV 1.00 (95% CI 0.54-1.00) and NPV 1.00 (95% CI 0.89-1.00). The authors conclude NGAL and KIM-1 have good diagnostic performance for malaria-associated AKI and that larger studies are needed to show superiority over creatinine.
papers.key_finding: At presentation, urine NGAL (AUROC 1.00) and urine KIM-1 predicted subsequent AKI in 39 imported falciparum patients (6 AKI cases); sample is small and the cohort non-endemic.
papers.corrections: PubMed record checked (efetch XML, 2026): no CommentsCorrections entries, so no erratum or retraction is listed. Publication types: Evaluation Study; Journal Article. Caution: n=39 with only 6 AKI events, so the perfect AUROC is likely optimistic; chosen because it is the human study that measures the same urinary NGAL and KIM-1 as the canine papers.

papers.title: Comparative Outcomes of Babesiosis in Immunocompromised and Nonimmunocompromised Hosts: A Multicenter Cohort Study.
papers.population_and_n: 225 adults with laboratory-confirmed babesiosis (2009-2023), multicentre US; 112 immunocompromised and/or asplenic/hyposplenic (ICAH) vs 113 immune-intact
papers.abstract_summary: Multicentre retrospective cohort of 225 adults (mean age 66 years, 36% female) with laboratory-confirmed babesiosis, comparing 112 patients with immunocompromise or asplenia/hyposplenia (ICAH) against immune-intact patients. ICAH patients had higher median peak parasitaemia (2.8% vs 0.9%, P<0.0001) and more complications, including AKI (24% vs 11%, P=0.016) and ARDS (11% vs 4%, P=0.041). They more often needed red cell transfusion (31% vs 17%) and exchange transfusion (18% vs 6%), had longer treatment (median 27 vs 10 days), and higher 12-month all-cause mortality (7% vs 1%) and recurrence (8% vs 0%). Haematological malignancy and B-cell-depleting therapy predicted recurrence. AKI is reported as a complication only; no kidney biomarkers or mechanism were examined.
papers.key_finding: In 225 human babesiosis patients, AKI occurred in 24% of immunocompromised/asplenic vs 11% of immune-intact patients, alongside higher peak parasitaemia and more ARDS.
papers.corrections: PubMed record checked (efetch XML, 2026): no CommentsCorrections entries, so no erratum or retraction is listed. No PMCID in record. Selected as the best-powered primary human babesiosis study with an explicit AKI outcome; it is not a mechanistic renal study, and the AKI definition is not stated in the abstract.

connections.shared_pathway: Early proximal tubular injury detectable in urine (NGAL, KIM-1) before or without a creatinine rise, in a haemoparasitic infection
connections.canine_evidence: CB024 (B. canis, n=42 infected vs 14 controls): urinary KIM-1, albumin, IgG, RBP and NAG raised, correlated with UPC, including in non-azotaemic dogs. CB103 (B. canis, n=22 vs 8 controls, TMT proteomics): urinary NGAL and L-FABP rose before azotaemia. CB124 (babesiosis and leptospirosis pooled): urinary NGAL and KIM-1 raised already in IRIS grade I AKI. CB053 (B. rossi, n=35 vs 10): tubular and glomerular markers raised and normalised by one month while creatinine/SDMA were unchanged. CB001 (B. canis, n=10 vs 10): urinary RBP and Tamm-Horsfall protein raised. All associational, small natural-infection cohorts.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 27612570: in 39 imported falciparum patients, urine NGAL (AUROC 1.00), serum NGAL and urine KIM-1 predicted AKI (6 events). Supporting alternates found but not selected as main papers: PMID 31966633 (autopsy kidneys, n=10 AKI/10 non-AKI/10 normal: proximal tubular KIM-1 and MMP-3 strongly raised in malarial AKI, correlated with creatinine and tubular necrosis) and PMID 40360328 (Indian severe falciparum cohort: plasma NGAL strongly associated with AKI severity). No human babesiosis study of NGAL/KIM-1 was found. PMID 39873391 reports AKI incidence in human babesiosis but no biomarkers.
connections.differences: Human evidence is from P. falciparum, not Babesia; no human babesiosis tubular-biomarker study was identified. Malaria involves cytoadherent sequestration, which Babesia lacks in the same form (B. rossi microvascular pathology in dogs is a partial analogue). Human NGAL study is a 39-patient pilot of non-immune travellers with only 6 AKI cases, so AUROC 1.00 is likely optimistic; canine cohorts are also small and define AKI by IRIS/creatinine/SDMA rather than KDIGO. Canine work measures urinary markers against healthy controls, not prediction of later AKI, and urinary NGAL/KIM-1 assays are species-specific. Dogs have recurring co-pathologies (glomerular injury, proteinuria) that human malaria papers measure less.
connections.strength_rationale: The same readouts (urinary NGAL and KIM-1 as markers of tubular injury preceding or accompanying creatinine rise) are measured in dogs with babesiosis and in humans with falciparum malaria, with concordant direction. The rating applies to the dog-to-malaria comparison; it is not demonstrated in human babesiosis, and the human sample is small, so conclusions should be limited to biomarker behaviour, not shared aetiology.

connections.shared_pathway: Intravascular haemolysis releasing cell-free haemoglobin, driving oxidative (lipid-peroxidation) injury to renal tubules
connections.canine_evidence: No REN-category canine study in the digest measured cell-free haemoglobin, haemoglobinuria or F2-isoprostanes against kidney outcome. Indirect only: CB083 (B. vogeli, natural infection) reported higher MDA, lower SOD and raised creatinine/urea versus uninfected dogs, but these are group-level co-findings and the digest does not state a linkage to AKI. CB154 (B. gibsoni, Mizoram) found higher LPO and lower GSH/T-AOC with multiorgan changes; LPO correlated with RBC count, not shown with renal indices. CB142 (B. gibsoni, 12 enrolled) found NAC adjunct improved antioxidant capacity only. CB097/CB080 necropsies showed haemosiderophage accumulation and congestion without kidney-specific mechanism. CB096 reports Coombs-positive haemolysis with azotaemia in one pup.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 28449641: in 107 severe falciparum malaria patients (58% AKI), plasma cell-free haemoglobin, F2-isoprostanes and isofurans were higher with AKI, correlated with haemolysis and parasite burden, independently associated with rising creatinine over 72 h, and F2-isoprostanes/isofurans/deformability were associated with later dialysis. A sepsis group (n=28) was included as a comparator. Supporting alternate: PMID 29872039 (P. knowlesi, n=48 severe/154 non-severe: CFHb rose with severity; AKI in 88% of severe cases; haemolysis-linked endothelial activation markers angiopoietin-2 and osteoprotegerin were independent AKI risk factors). For human babesiosis, PMID 39873391 gives AKI rates and higher parasitaemia in ICAH patients but no CFH or oxidative-stress data.
connections.differences: Canine babesiosis haemolysis includes an immune-mediated component (e.g. Coombs-positive cases such as CB096) and, in B. rossi, haemolysis that is not strictly proportional to parasitaemia; malaria haemolysis is parasite-burden-linked with pitting and red cell rigidity. Malaria AKI studies have a sepsis comparator and serial creatinine; canine studies lack CFH and use cross-sectional sampling. Haemoglobinuria is a recognised feature in some canine babesiosis (not quantified in digest REN entries) but is not measured as exposure in any listed canine study. P. falciparum sequestration contributes microvascular obstruction absent in B. microti. Antioxidant markers in dogs are systemic and not tied to renal outcome.
connections.strength_rationale: Human data directly link CFH and lipid peroxidation to AKI in malaria. Canine babesiosis shows haemolysis, oxidative-stress shifts and tubular injury biomarkers, but no canine study in the digest measured CFH or tested the CFH-to-tubular-injury pathway. The link is therefore inferred, not demonstrated in dogs or in human babesiosis.

connections.shared_pathway: AKI as a correlate of high-severity babesiosis with multi-organ dysfunction (ARDS) and worse outcome, with host risk factors for severe disease
connections.canine_evidence: CB025 (B. rossi, n=152 records): renal azotaemia in 14% (21/152), associated with collapse, hypoglycaemia, cerebral babesiosis, ARDS and lower survival; USG <1.030 missed most. CB061 (B. canis, n=240): creatinine >5 mg/dL associated with death; mortality 33.9% with renal involvement. CB119 (narrative review): B. rossi ranked most pathogenic, B. gibsoni and B. vogeli less so. Association only; none relates renal injury to parasitaemia or to splenic status.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 39873391 (n=225): AKI 24% in immunocompromised/asplenic vs 11% in immune-intact patients, with higher peak parasitaemia (2.8% vs 0.9%) and more ARDS (11% vs 4%) and mortality (7% vs 1% at 12 months). PMID 41666444 (TriNetX, 1,566 PCR-confirmed cases, 159 with sepsis; AKI listed among complications; read as abstract only, not selected as it is coded-data and AKI counts are not given in the abstract).
connections.differences: Dogs are mostly immunocompetent hosts infected by different species (B. rossi, B. canis, B. gibsoni, B. vogeli) than B. microti, B. divergens or B. duncani in humans. Human cohort is older adults (mean age 66) with comorbidities; the canine cohorts are not selected by splenic status or immunosuppression. AKI definitions differ (KDIGO-type vs IRIS/azotaemia thresholds); canine retrospective cohorts use admission creatinine and may miss non-azotaemic injury. Treatment differs (human exchange transfusion and atovaquone-azithromycin vs imidocarb/diminazene). Neither dataset isolates renal mechanism.
connections.strength_rationale: Both hosts show AKI co-occurring with ARDS and higher mortality in severe babesiosis, but this is a shared clinical association. No study in either host measured a common renal mechanism, and parasitaemia/asplenia as drivers of AKI is demonstrated only at group level in humans and not at all in dogs.

papers.title: Pulmonary Manifestations of Babesiosis and Predictors of Mortality from a Quaternary Care Center in Westchester, New York.
papers.population_and_n: 147 hospitalised adults with confirmed babesiosis (63 severe, 41 ICU, 10 deaths), Westchester Medical Center, New York, 2006-2023; single-centre retrospective
papers.abstract_summary: This single-centre retrospective study reviewed 147 hospitalised adults with confirmed babesiosis (2006-2023) to describe pulmonary involvement, using logistic regression for factors tied to severe disease and death. Of the 147, 63 were severe, 41 needed ICU care and 10 died. Respiratory symptoms (cough, dyspnoea, oxygen need, respiratory failure) occurred in 42%, and 55 patients had abnormal chest radiographs (infiltrates, effusions). Parasitaemia of 10% or more was present in 75% of severe cases. Severe disease was associated with age 70 or older, severe dyspnoea, radiographic abnormality, WBC above 5000, haemoglobin 8 g/dL or lower and raised creatinine. Mortality was associated with age 70 or older, encephalopathy, acute kidney injury, severe dyspnoea at admission, abnormal chest radiograph and intubation. Exchange transfusion did not correlate with outcome. Lyme seropositivity was 28%. The authors conclude that pulmonary symptoms and abnormal radiographs are common and signal worse outcomes.
papers.key_finding: In 147 hospitalised babesiosis adults, 42% had respiratory symptoms; abnormal chest radiograph, severe dyspnoea and intubation were associated with mortality, as was concurrent acute kidney injury.
papers.corrections: No CommentsCorrections entries (errata, retraction or correction notices) in the PubMed XML record for PMID 40333147, checked 2026-10-23.

papers.title: Babesiosis as a cause of acute respiratory distress syndrome: a series of eight cases.
papers.population_and_n: 22 adult B. microti patients admitted to a medical ICU (Lower Hudson Valley, New York, 2008-2016); 8 developed ARDS; retrospective
papers.abstract_summary: The authors reviewed adults admitted to a tertiary-hospital medical ICU in New York between 2008 and 2016 to describe ARDS complicating Babesia microti infection. Of 22 babesiosis ICU patients, 8 (36.4%) had ARDS. Six of the 8 (75%) developed ARDS after anti-babesial therapy had started, although those patients also had longer symptom duration before treatment than the two who developed ARDS earlier (7.5 vs 4.5 days, p=0.34). Three of the 8 (37.5%) died without ARDS resolution, versus 14.3% mortality among the 14 patients without ARDS (p=0.31). Survivors tended to be younger (54.6 vs 74.0 years, p=0.07), and 3 of 5 survivors avoided mechanical ventilation. Non-survivors had markedly higher SOFA scores (12.3 vs 6.0, p=0.0006). The authors raise, but cannot resolve, whether parasite killing contributes to ARDS onset.
papers.key_finding: 8 of 22 ICU babesiosis patients developed ARDS, mostly after antiparasitic therapy began (confounded by longer symptom duration); 3 of 8 died.
papers.corrections: No CommentsCorrections entries (errata, retraction or correction notices) in the PubMed XML record for PMID 30585748, checked 2026-10-23. No PMC full text. Small retrospective series; the mortality difference (37.5% vs 14.3%) was not significant.

papers.title: Release of endothelial activation markers in lungs of patients with malaria-associated acute respiratory distress syndrome.
papers.study_type: primary human cohort (post-mortem case-control immunohistochemistry); comparator pathogen, not babesiosis
papers.population_and_n: Post-mortem lung sections from Thai P. falciparum patients with alveolar oedema (MA-ARDS), P. falciparum patients without alveolar oedema, and uninfected accidental-death controls; group sizes not reported in abstract
papers.abstract_summary: Malaria-associated ARDS (MA-ARDS) is poorly understood. Because endothelial activation drives other malarial complications, the authors stained post-mortem lung sections for von Willebrand factor (VWF) and angiopoietin-2 (ANG-2) in three groups: P. falciparum patients without alveolar oedema, P. falciparum patients with alveolar oedema (MA-ARDS), and uninfected controls with normal lungs, using semi-quantitative scoring. Oedematous alveoli and intravascular VWF and ANG-2 staining were significantly higher in MA-ARDS than in both control groups. VWF in alveolar septa and the lining of large vessels was lower in MA-ARDS, which the authors interpret as Weibel-Palade body release. ANG-2 was raised in the septa of infected patients without oedema, and ANG-2-positive leukocytes were increased in alveoli in both infected groups. The data indicate marked pulmonary endothelial activation in MA-ARDS.
papers.key_finding: Post-mortem lungs from falciparum patients with alveolar oedema showed raised VWF and ANG-2 in oedematous alveoli, indicating pulmonary endothelial activation and Weibel-Palade body release.
papers.corrections: No CommentsCorrections entries (errata, retraction or correction notices) in the PubMed XML record for PMID 31796023, checked 2026-10-23. Group sizes not stated in the abstract; semi-quantitative IHC on post-mortem tissue, so cause-effect cannot be inferred.

connections.shared_pathway: Acute alveolar-capillary injury leading to non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema and ARDS in severe haemoprotozoan disease
connections.canine_evidence: CB111 (2023, B. rossi, necropsy/IHC, n not reported in abstract): fatal natural infection showed alveolar oedema and acute interstitial pneumonia with fibrin and increased macrophages and T cells, partly overlapping exudative diffuse alveolar damage. CB102 (2022, single puppy, B. canis vogeli): hypoxaemic respiratory failure, suspected ARDS, survived with lung-protective ventilation and neuromuscular blockade. CB025 (2018, B. rossi, n=152): ARDS was associated with renal azotaemia and lower survival. CB079, CB097 and CB032 are single-animal reports of non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. CB080 (n=6) proposed circulatory failure rather than primary lung injury as the cause of death. Canine ARDS is thus described, but lung injury mechanism was examined only histologically in CB111, and no study measured lung permeability, BAL or endothelial markers.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 30585748 (ICU series): 8 of 22 B. microti ICU patients (36.4%) developed ARDS, 3 of 8 died; SOFA was much higher in non-survivors. PMID 40333147 (n=147): 42% had respiratory symptoms, 55 had abnormal chest radiographs, and severe dyspnoea, abnormal radiograph, intubation and acute kidney injury were associated with mortality. Neither human babesiosis paper examined lung histology or molecular markers. PMID 31796023 (malaria): post-mortem falciparum lungs with alveolar oedema showed increased VWF and ANG-2 in oedematous alveoli.
connections.differences: Canine data are mostly necropsy and case reports. Human babesiosis data are B. microti in older, often comorbid New York adults, some splenectomised or immunocompromised; the dogs were B. rossi, B. canis, B. gibsoni and B. vogeli. P. falciparum sequesters in the microvasculature, which Babesia does not do to the same extent, so malaria is a comparator, not an equivalent. Human series are retrospective, small and confounded by Lyme coinfection (28% seropositive in PMID 40333147), age and treatment, and the ARDS definition differs between hosts. Canine ARDS is mostly 'suspected' in the digest, with no Berlin-criteria equivalent.
connections.strength_rationale: The same clinical syndrome (ARDS or non-cardiogenic oedema with respiratory failure, associated with severity and mortality) is documented in both hosts, and canine DAD-like histology (CB111) fits the ARDS concept. However, the alveolar-capillary injury mechanism is not measured in human babesiosis, and the only mechanistic human lung data are from malaria. Clinical ARDS alone does not establish a shared pathway, so the rating stops at plausible.

connections.shared_pathway: Pulmonary endothelial activation (VWF, angiopoietin-2) and leukocyte-mediated inflammation as drivers of alveolar permeability
connections.canine_evidence: CB111 (2023, B. rossi, necropsy/IHC): increased pulmonary macrophages and T cells with fibrin and partial DAD overlap. This is the only canine measurement of lung inflammatory cells. No canine study in the digest measured VWF, ANG-2, neutrophil activation or any other endothelial marker in lung, and CB080 (n=6) favoured circulatory failure over lung injury.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 31796023 (malaria post-mortem lungs): VWF and ANG-2 increased in oedematous alveoli and intravascular VWF raised in MA-ARDS, with ANG-2-positive leukocytes increased in alveoli of infected patients; the authors read this as Weibel-Palade body release. No human babesiosis paper identified in this search measured endothelial activation in lung. PMID 30585748 and PMID 40333147 report clinical data only.
connections.differences: Evidence is post-mortem, semi-quantitative IHC, with group sizes not stated in the abstract, in P. falciparum (a sequestering parasite). Canine babesiosis, especially B. rossi, is often described as a systemic inflammatory response with haemolysis, and endothelial activation may contribute, but this is not shown in the lung. The canine macrophage and T-cell infiltrate is a different cell readout from the human VWF and ANG-2 findings, so the data are not like-for-like.
connections.strength_rationale: The human endothelial-activation evidence is from malaria only, and the canine lung data measure different cell types and no endothelial markers. A shared endothelial mechanism in babesiosis is a hypothesis that fits the clinical picture, not something demonstrated in either babesiosis host.

connections.shared_pathway: Pulmonary injury emerging after antiparasitic treatment, possibly linked to parasite killing and release of inflammatory mediators, with kidney injury as a co-occurring severity marker
connections.canine_evidence: No canine study in the digest PUL sections reports timing of lung injury relative to antiparasitic therapy. CB102 (single puppy) is descriptive and does not establish treatment-relative onset or causation. CB025 (n=152, B. rossi) found renal azotaemia associated with ARDS and lower survival, supporting multi-organ co-occurrence but not a treatment-timing effect.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 30585748: 6 of 8 babesiosis ARDS cases (75%) began after anti-babesial therapy started, though symptom duration before treatment was longer in that group (7.5 vs 4.5 days, p=0.34), and the authors state the confounding. PMID 40333147: acute kidney injury and intubation were associated with mortality in the same cohort in which respiratory involvement was common. PMID 31796023 provides no timing information.
connections.differences: Post-treatment pulmonary oedema is well known in severe falciparum malaria but is not demonstrated by the papers selected here (see also PMID 39448997, an alternate not selected, in which 9 of 56 severe falciparum patients developed clinical pulmonary oedema after admission). The human timing signal is retrospective and confounded, and the canine literature has no timing data. Dogs are treated with imidocarb and other regimens, versus atovaquone-azithromycin or clindamycin-quinine in humans, and dogs have no equivalent of exchange-transfusion practice.
connections.strength_rationale: The treatment-timing association appears only in a small retrospective human series and is explicitly confounded; no canine study reports it. Renal co-involvement (CB025 and PMID 40333147) is an association, not a pathway demonstrated in both hosts.
