Q6 malaria[tiab] AND (ARDS OR "respiratory distress" OR "lung injury" OR pulmonary[ti]) AND 2014-2026[dp]: 360 hits; screened to find human studies.
Q7 (malaria OR falciparum OR vivax OR knowlesi in title) AND respiratory/lung/ARDS/pulmonary in title: 307 hits; first 80 titles screened. Human primary candidates seen: PMID 39150978 (P. knowlesi ALI, n=213), 39448997 (falciparum pulmonary oedema biomarkers, 56 severe), 37375081 (Berlin imported falciparum, n=536), 31796023 (post-mortem lung IHC), 40767696 (single ECMO case).
Q8 (Babesia OR babesiosis) AND (autopsy OR histopatholog* OR diffuse alveolar damage) AND (human OR patient): 26 hits; no human babesiosis lung histology paper found (hits were veterinary, rodent or non-lung).
Q9 (malaria OR falciparum) AND (autopsy OR "diffuse alveolar damage" OR "alveolar-capillary" OR "pulmonary permeability") AND (lung OR pulmonary): 69 hits; surfaced 31796023 and 32185202 (SphK1/S1PR3 in falciparum lung, not selected).
Effective query count: 9 (slightly over the ~8 target).

Selection rationale: (1) 40333147 is the largest recent primary human babesiosis dataset with explicit pulmonary outcomes (n=147, 2025). (2) 30585748 is the only human babesiosis study dedicated to ARDS with a denominator (8/22 ICU patients), older than 2016 criterion no, it is 2018-2019 so within range; it is a small case series. (3) 31796023 is the best human lung-compartment mechanistic malaria study (post-mortem IHC), matching the canine necropsy focus of CB111. Alternates considered but not selected for the three-paper limit: 39150978 (strong, n=213, neutrophil activation and ALI in knowlesi malaria, associated with ANG-2; good second malaria paper if a fourth is allowed), 39448997 (biomarkers did not predict pulmonary oedema), 37375081 (fluid intake and shock as risk factors for respiratory distress), 36411784 (case report and review). Abstracts were read in full from efetch text output; bibliographic data (volume, issue, pages, DOI, PMCID, dates) were checked in the PubMed XML records. CommentsCorrections check: none present on 40333147, 30585748, 39150978 and 31796023 (39150978 was checked but not selected). Limitations: no human babesiosis paper measures lung histology or endothelial markers, so mechanistic comparison relies on malaria; Williams 2025 and Alvarez De Leon 2019 are from the same New York institution and partly overlap in era (2006-2023 vs 2008-2016), so cases may overlap and should not be pooled."

papers.title: Alteration of Blood Lactate Levels in Severe Falciparum Malaria: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.population_and_n: 30 studies of patients with severe falciparum malaria (pooled n = 30,202 cases); 9 studies compared severe with uncomplicated malaria (1568 vs 1693 cases); 6 studies compared deaths (272) with survivors (1370).
papers.abstract_summary: The review asked whether blood lactate, the usual driver of metabolic acidosis in severe malaria, is higher in severe than uncomplicated disease and higher in patients who die. PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus were searched (793 records retrieved, 30 included), with quality appraised by the Jadad scale and STROBE, and random-effects pooling with meta-regression and subgroup analysis. Pooled mean lactate in severe malaria was 5.04 mM (95% CI 4.44-5.64; I2 99.9%). Lactate was higher in severe than uncomplicated malaria (mean difference 2.46 mM; 95% CI 0.85-4.07; nine studies) and higher in fatal than surviving severe malaria (mean difference 2.74 mM; 95% CI 1.74-3.75; I2 95.8%; six studies). The authors conclude lactate differs markedly by severity and outcome, and call for studies of its prognostic value for identifying patients at high risk of developing severe malaria or dying.
papers.key_finding: Blood lactate was about 2.7 mM higher in patients who died of severe falciparum malaria than in survivors (six studies), with very high heterogeneity.
papers.corrections: PubMed record checked 2026-10-23 (efetch XML): no CommentsCorrections entries (no erratum, retraction or expression of concern). Publication type Journal Article/Review; the abstract describes a systematic review and meta-analysis. Chosen as a review (not a primary study) because it pools 30 studies and is the only paper that directly pools the survivor versus non-survivor lactate contrast; heterogeneity (I2 about 96-100%) limits precision of the pooled estimates. Primary alternatives reviewed: PMID 38243243 (n=1674 children, cerebral malaria, admission lactate >5 mmol/L OR 2.49 for death) and PMID 34172046 (n=5425 children, AQUAMAT secondary analysis, hypoglycaemia OR 5.16 for severe metabolic acidosis).

papers.title: Cortisol and adrenal androgens as independent predictors of mortality in septic patients.
papers.population_and_n: 139 consecutive adults with severe sepsis or septic shock, Spain (prospective cohort; hormones measured within 24 h of onset).
papers.abstract_summary: This prospective single-country cohort tested whether basal cortisol, DHEA, DHEAS and their ratios predict mortality in septic patients. Hormones were sampled in the first 24 h; ROC analysis and adjusted logistic regression assessed in-hospital, 28-day and 90-day death, with comparison against lactate, CRP, SOFA and APACHE II. Cortisol was the best predictor, with AUCs of 0.758 (in-hospital), 0.759 (28-day) and 0.705 (90-day), whereas for 28-day mortality SOFA, APACHE II, lactate and CRP gave AUCs of 0.644, 0.618, 0.643 and 0.647. Cortisol above 17.5 ug/dL carried adjusted odds ratios of about 10.1 (in-hospital) and 9.5 (28-day) for death. Adrenal androgen associations were weak; the cortisol/DHEAS ratio was the best 90-day predictor (AUC 0.737). Cortisol was concluded to be the strongest early prognostic marker.
papers.key_finding: Admission cortisol above 17.5 ug/dL predicted in-hospital and 28-day death (adjusted OR about 10) and outperformed SOFA, APACHE II and lactate in 139 septic patients.
papers.corrections: PubMed record checked 2026-10-23: no CommentsCorrections entries (no erratum or retraction). Sepsis (non-parasitic) cohort, so a comparator for hypercortisolaemia as a mortality marker, not an equivalent of babesiosis; single cohort of moderate size, no external validation. Larger or newer sepsis cortisol studies exist (e.g. PMID 42617202, 2026, multicentre retrospective) but were not read in full.

papers.title: Thyroid hormone levels as a predictor marker predict the prognosis of patients with sepsis.
papers.population_and_n: 929 adult septic patients identified from the MIMIC-III intensive care database (703 favourable and 226 unfavourable outcome); retrospective database analysis.
papers.abstract_summary: Using the MIMIC-III critical-care database, the authors identified 929 septic patients to test whether admission thyroid hormone levels relate to short-term outcome. Variables with P below 0.1 on univariate analysis entered a multivariable binary logistic regression, and discrimination was assessed by AUROC. Thyroxine (T4) was significantly lower in patients with an unfavourable outcome (P < 0.01), and lower admission T4 was associated with poor outcome (OR 0.556, 95% CI 0.41-0.75). A combined model of free T4, T4 and SAPS II reached an AUROC of 0.82 for ICU survival, above free T4 alone (0.65), T4 alone (0.71) and SAPS II (0.70-0.72), so thyroid hormones added predictive information to the clinical score. The authors conclude low serum T4 is a predictive marker of short-term sepsis outcome.
papers.key_finding: Lower admission thyroxine was independently associated with poor short-term outcome in 929 septic patients, and added to SAPS II in a combined model (AUROC 0.82).
papers.corrections: PubMed record checked 2026-10-23: no CommentsCorrections entries (no erratum or retraction); no PMCID in the record. Retrospective database study with limited detail on thyroid-testing selection (hormones measured only in a subset of patients is likely but not stated in the abstract). The abstract does not report TSH; for the TSH-unchanged point, a separate sepsis study (PMID 41827956, n=149, 2026) and a meta-analysis (PMID 30237537, 2018) were read but not selected.

connections.shared_pathway: Hyperlactataemia and metabolic (lactic) acidosis from tissue hypoperfusion/hypoxia, as a marker of death in a haemolytic, microvascular parasitic disease
connections.canine_evidence: CB074 (B. gibsoni, prognostic case-control, n=108 dogs plus 30 controls): lactate, urea and ALT were specific prognostic markers, and a discriminant score predicted lethal outcome with 79% sensitivity and 83% specificity (survivor/non-survivor split not given in the abstract). CB068 (B. canis, n=14 vs 10 controls): half the dogs had mixed acid-base disorders including lactate/chloride-related acidosis alongside respiratory alkalosis. CB082 (experimental B. rossi, n=5): acidosis and inflammation reproduced with dose-dependent severity.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 34827078: in a meta-analysis of 30 severe falciparum malaria studies (n=30,202), pooled lactate was 5.04 mM, 2.46 mM higher than in uncomplicated malaria (nine studies) and 2.74 mM higher in fatal than surviving cases (six studies; 272 deaths vs 1370 survivors; I2 about 96%). The review itself notes that the prognostic value of lactate still needs study. No human babesiosis study measuring lactate or acid-base status was found.
connections.differences: Human evidence is from P. falciparum malaria (mostly African children and adults), not human babesiosis; sequestration of infected red cells in the microvasculature is a defining mechanism in falciparum malaria and has not been shown for Babesia canis in the same way (CB041 is only a narrative proposal), so the cause of lactate rise may differ (anaemia/hypoxia and hypoperfusion vs obstruction). Canine lactate prognostic data come from B. gibsoni (CB074) while the acid-base descriptions come from B. canis and B. rossi, so no single canine study matches the pooled human contrast. Canine studies are small and associational; the human pooled estimates are very heterogeneous. Splenic status, treatment (artesunate vs imidocarb) and point-of-care lactate methods differ.
connections.strength_rationale: The same measurement (blood lactate) and the same contrast (higher in non-survivors than survivors) are reported in dogs with babesiosis (CB074) and in pooled severe malaria data (PMID 34827078). The claim is limited to this prognostic association; a shared causal mechanism for the lactate rise is not shown, and the human data are not from babesiosis.

connections.shared_pathway: Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal activation: raised cortisol that tracks severity and discriminates non-survivors
connections.canine_evidence: CB040 (B. rossi, n=320 PCR-confirmed dogs): many variables were associated with death but none was an independent multivariate predictor; high cortisol (with low T4, high bilirubin and urea) discriminated best. CB105 (experimental B. rossi, n=5 Beagles, two inocula): cortisol rose in step with severity and inoculum dose. CB083 (B. vogeli, natural infection, group sizes ambiguous): higher plasma cortisol than uninfected dogs, with lower glucose.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 30946764: in 139 patients with severe sepsis or septic shock, basal cortisol in the first 24 h was the best mortality predictor (AUC 0.758 in-hospital, 0.759 at 28 days), better than lactate (0.643), SOFA (0.644) and APACHE II (0.618); cortisol above 17.5 ug/dL gave adjusted OR about 10 for in-hospital death. No human babesiosis or malaria cohort selected here reports cortisol as an outcome predictor.
connections.differences: Human comparator is bacterial/viral sepsis in ICU patients, not a parasitic haemolytic infection; the malaria literature (e.g. PMID 37492570, children with severe malaria, higher cortisol in severe than uncomplicated disease with reduced glucocorticoid sensitivity) was read but not selected and is not used as evidence here. Canine cortisol was not an independent predictor in CB040 once multivariable analysis was applied, whereas the human study reports independent associations; canine sampling (single time point, sometimes after supportive care) and assay differ; CB105 has n=5. Dogs and humans differ in cortisol binding and in corticosteroid use before sampling.
connections.strength_rationale: Raised cortisol is measured in both hosts and associated with death (CB040 univariate discrimination; PMID 30946764 adjusted OR and AUC), and CB105 shows a severity/dose gradient experimentally. The strength label applies to the association only; canine evidence is weaker (no independent predictor), the human host here is sepsis rather than malaria or babesiosis, and the adrenal mechanism (stress response vs adrenal insufficiency or glucocorticoid resistance) is not tested in dogs.

connections.shared_pathway: Non-thyroidal illness: low circulating thyroxine with TSH not raised, falling with severity and predicting death
connections.canine_evidence: CB040 (B. rossi, n=320): low T4 was among the variables that discriminated death best, although no independent multivariate predictor emerged. CB105 (experimental B. rossi, n=5): T4 fell with severity and inoculum dose while TSH stayed within reference limits. A B. canis thyroid study (n=60) was not used because only its title was accessible.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 33652253: in 929 septic patients (MIMIC-III), T4 was significantly lower in those with unfavourable outcome (P<0.01); lower admission T4 carried OR 0.556 (95% CI 0.41-0.75) for poor outcome, and a combined fT4, T4 and SAPS II model reached AUROC 0.82 for ICU survival, above SAPS II alone. No human babesiosis study of thyroid hormones was found.
connections.differences: Human evidence is from sepsis (retrospective database analysis with unmeasured selection of who had thyroid tests), not babesiosis or malaria; where malaria has been examined (PMID 38270243, uncomplicated paediatric falciparum malaria, n=90 cases) free T3 was raised rather than lowered, with fT4 unchanged, so the direction of thyroid change is not uniform across parasitic diseases and was not selected as evidence. Canine studies measured total T4 (the digest does not say which fractions) and the dog is a species in which non-thyroidal illness effects on T4 are well documented but with different binding proteins; canine data include an experimental model of only five dogs. Neither CB040 nor the human study shows that low T4 is causal rather than a marker of illness severity.
connections.strength_rationale: The same analyte (T4) is lower in more severe or fatal disease in dogs with babesiosis (CB040, CB105) and in septic patients (PMID 33652253), and the TSH-unchanged feature is reported in CB105 (the human study abstract does not report TSH). The finding is an association with severity/outcome only, and the human host is a sepsis comparator, not a haemoparasitic infection.

papers.title: Parasite histones are toxic to brain endothelium and link blood barrier breakdown and thrombosis in cerebral malaria.
papers.population_and_n: Malawian children with cerebral malaria (P. falciparum): circulating histones in patient serum, brain MRI, postmortem brain sections, plus in vitro human brain endothelial assays. Exact n is not stated in the abstract and was not verified from full text.
papers.abstract_summary: The authors ask how P. falciparum causes the endothelial disruption seen in paediatric cerebral malaria, where microvascular thrombosis and blood-brain barrier (BBB) breakdown are linked to fatal brain swelling. Circulating extracellular histones, of host and parasite origin in roughly equal measure, were significantly raised in cerebral malaria patients, and higher levels went with brain swelling on MRI. In postmortem brain sections, histones co-localised with infected erythrocytes sequestered in small vessels, which suggests local release at schizont rupture. Luminal histone staining coincided with thrombosis and vascular leakage. Patient sera and purified parasite histones disrupted barrier function and killed cultured human brain endothelial cells. Anti-histone antibody and non-anticoagulant heparin blocked this effect. The authors propose histones as a link between sequestration, thrombosis, BBB breakdown and brain swelling.
papers.key_finding: Histone levels tracked MRI brain swelling, and postmortem histone staining colocalised with sequestered parasitised cells, thrombosis and vascular leakage in human cerebral malaria brain.
papers.corrections: No CommentsCorrections elements (erratum, retraction or correction links) in the PubMed XML record, checked 2026-10-23. Bibliographic data verified from the PubMed record.

papers.title: Increased brain microvascular hemoglobin concentrations in children with cerebral malaria.
papers.population_and_n: 46 Malawian children with cerebral malaria (Blantyre coma score of 2 or less, retinopathy-positive); comparators 33 with uncomplicated malaria and 29 healthy children
papers.abstract_summary: Brain swelling is linked to death in cerebral malaria, but it is unclear whether it reflects cerebral oedema or vascular congestion, which affect tissue haemoglobin differently. Using near-infrared spectroscopy, the authors measured cerebral microvascular haemoglobin concentration in 46 Malawian children with cerebral malaria, 33 with uncomplicated malaria and 29 healthy children. Concentrations were higher in cerebral malaria than in uncomplicated malaria (median 145.2 vs 82.9 uM, P = 0.008) and correlated with the MRI brain swelling score (r = 0.37, P = 0.03). Detrended fluctuation analysis showed lower self-similarity of the haemoglobin signal in cerebral malaria (0.63 vs 0.91, P < 0.0001), which suggests impaired cerebral blood flow regulation. The authors conclude that excess blood volume, possibly from vascular congestion, may contribute to brain swelling.
papers.key_finding: Cerebral microvascular haemoglobin was higher in paediatric cerebral malaria and correlated modestly with MRI brain swelling (r=0.37), which suggests vascular congestion contributes to swelling.
papers.corrections: No CommentsCorrections elements (erratum, retraction or correction links) in the PubMed XML record, checked 2026-10-23. Bibliographic data verified from the PubMed record.

papers.title: Neurologic Complications of Babesiosis, United States, 2011-2021.
papers.population_and_n: 163 adults hospitalised with laboratory-confirmed babesiosis at Yale-New Haven Hospital, Connecticut, USA, January 2011 to October 2021 (retrospective record review)
papers.abstract_summary: Babesiosis is caused by intraerythrocytic protozoa and its full neurologic spectrum, underlying neuropathophysiology and risk factors are poorly understood. The authors reviewed the medical records of adults admitted to Yale-New Haven Hospital with laboratory-confirmed babesiosis between January 2011 and October 2021. Among 163 patients, more than half had at least one neurologic symptom during admission. The most frequent symptoms were headache, confusion or delirium, and impaired consciousness. Neurologic symptoms were associated with high-grade parasitaemia, renal failure and a history of diabetes mellitus. The authors advise clinicians in endemic areas to recognise neurologic presentations of babesiosis. The study describes frequency and associations only and does not measure any mechanism such as sequestration, imaging change or barrier disruption.
papers.key_finding: Over half of 163 hospitalised babesiosis patients had neurologic symptoms, associated with high-grade parasitaemia, renal failure and diabetes; no mechanism was assessed.
papers.corrections: No CommentsCorrections elements (erratum, retraction or correction links) in the PubMed XML record, checked 2026-10-23. Bibliographic data verified from the PubMed record. Species is not given in the abstract (US babesiosis is overwhelmingly B. microti, which is an inference, not a stated fact). Not a mechanistic study.

connections.shared_pathway: Microvascular sequestration and vascular congestion in the brain as a driver of brain swelling
connections.canine_evidence: Canine data do not measure brain swelling, brain imaging or brain sequestration. CB041 (2019, B. canis, narrative review largely of the author's own experimental model) proposes that infected erythrocytes sequester in capillaries through endothelial attachment, so that severe disease occurs despite low circulating parasitaemia; this is a hypothesis, not a canine brain measurement. CB080 (2021, B. canis, necropsy of 6 dogs) found multi-organ congestion, oedema and effusions and the authors proposed circulatory failure as the cause of death; the digest does not say the brain was examined. CB116 (2023, experimental B. vogeli superinfection in E. canis-exposed Beagles, n=18) reported histological lesions in the brain among other organs. CB069 (2020, n=7 dogs per group) described a clinical entity, 'cerebral babesiosis', with raised serum manganese (associational).
connections.human_evidence: PMID 32579667: in paediatric cerebral malaria, postmortem brain sections showed parasitised erythrocytes sequestered in small vessels, and circulating histone levels were associated with MRI brain swelling. PMID 37703350: cerebral microvascular haemoglobin by NIRS was higher in 46 children with cerebral malaria than in uncomplicated malaria and correlated with MRI swelling score (r=0.37), which suggests vascular congestion contributes. PMID 37209667: more than half of 163 hospitalised babesiosis patients had neurologic symptoms, but no sequestration or imaging data.
connections.differences: The human mechanistic data are from P. falciparum in African children. P. falciparum sequesters through PfEMP1-mediated cytoadherence (EPCR binding, per PMID 34549725, which was read but not selected). Babesia has no PfEMP1; B. canis encodes VESA proteins (103 predicted in CB010), but no canine study here shows brain-specific adherence. Plasmodium schizont rupture is the proposed histone source in PMID 32579667; Babesia replicates by a different division process (general knowledge, not from the retrieved records). The human babesiosis study is of adults, probably B. microti, and many such patients have splenic or comorbid risk factors. Dogs vary in species (B. rossi, B. canis, B. vogeli, B. gibsoni), and the canine 'cerebral babesiosis' definition is clinical. Brain sequestration in dogs has not been shown by the canine papers in the digest.
connections.strength_rationale: Brain sequestration and congestion causing swelling are demonstrated in human cerebral malaria. In dogs, only a sequestration hypothesis (CB041), non-specific multi-organ congestion (CB080) and brain histological lesions in an experimental model (CB116) are reported, so the same mechanism has not been measured in the canine brain.

connections.shared_pathway: Endothelial activation, microthrombosis and blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption
connections.canine_evidence: The canine evidence is systemic, not brain-specific. CB004 (2017, B. canis, n=30 dogs vs 10 controls) showed raised thrombomodulin, HMGB-1, VCAM-1 and suPAR, which indicates endothelial activation and altered fibrinolysis. CB145 (2026, B. rossi, n=97 dogs, 12 non-survivors with necropsy) reported platelet activation, factor consumption, fibrinolytic shutdown and fibrin microthrombi as part of thromboinflammation. CB011 (2017, n=25) found a procoagulant state. None of these assessed BBB permeability, CSF protein or brain endothelium in dogs.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 32579667: patient sera and purified parasite histones disrupted barrier function in cultured human brain endothelial cells, and luminal vascular histone staining in postmortem cerebral malaria brain colocalised with thrombosis and leakage. Anti-histone antibody and non-anticoagulant heparin blocked the effect in vitro.
connections.differences: The human barrier evidence comes from postmortem tissue and in vitro assays in P. falciparum cerebral malaria. Canine data are blood biomarkers and necropsy fibrin microthrombi from whole-body disease, with no BBB-specific endpoint. A systemic thromboinflammatory state in canine babesiosis (similar to severe malaria or sepsis) does not show that the barrier fails in the brain. Source of histones is unclear in Babesia. Therapeutic inference (heparin) cannot be drawn for dogs from these data.
connections.strength_rationale: Endothelial activation and microthrombi are measured in both hosts, but only at the systemic level in dogs, and BBB breakdown has been shown only in human cerebral malaria.

connections.shared_pathway: Neurologic involvement associated with high parasite burden and concurrent renal failure
connections.canine_evidence: CB025 (2018, B. rossi, n=152 dogs, retrospective analysis of three prospective datasets) found renal azotaemia in 14% (21/152), associated with collapse, hypoglycaemia, cerebral babesiosis, ARDS and lower survival (associational). CB141 (2025, B. canis, n=342) found that parasitaemia and CRP correlated positively with haematological severity, but not specifically with neurologic signs.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 37209667: among 163 hospitalised babesiosis patients, neurologic symptoms (headache, confusion or delirium, impaired consciousness) were associated with high-grade parasitaemia, renal failure and diabetes mellitus.
connections.differences: Both associations are cross-sectional and confounded by overall disease severity; uraemia, hypoglycaemia, hypoxia and metabolic derangements can cause encephalopathy without any parasite-specific brain process. Human cohort is adult, hospitalised, probably B. microti (inference) with comorbidities such as diabetes; canine data are B. rossi with 'cerebral babesiosis' defined clinically. The canine parasitaemia-severity link (CB141) is not neurologic, so the parasite-burden link to neurologic signs is shown only in humans.
connections.strength_rationale: A similar association of neurologic signs with renal failure is reported in both hosts, but both are associational, neither isolates a brain-specific mechanism, and the parasite-burden link to neurologic signs is shown only in humans.

papers.title: Cardiac Complications of Human Babesiosis.
papers.study_type: primary human cohort (retrospective single-centre record review)
papers.population_and_n: 163 adult inpatients with smear- and/or PCR-confirmed babesiosis, Yale-New Haven Hospital, Jan 2011 to Oct 2021
papers.abstract_summary: The authors reviewed records of all adults admitted with confirmed babesiosis to one US hospital over about ten years. Of 163 patients, 32 (19.6%) had at least one cardiac complication in hospital. The commonest were atrial fibrillation (9.4%), heart failure (8.6%), QTc prolongation (8.0%) and cardiac ischaemia (6.8%). Neither cardiovascular risk factors nor pre-existing cardiac disease were significantly associated with developing a cardiac complication. Patients with a cardiac complication more often had high-grade parasitaemia (>10%), and had longer hospital and ICU stays and higher mortality than those without. The authors conclude that cardiac complications are common in acute babesiosis and that the link between babesiosis severity and cardiac outcomes needs further study. The abstract does not report troponin values or echocardiographic data.
papers.key_finding: About one in five hospitalised babesiosis patients had a cardiac complication, associated with parasitaemia >10%, ICU stay and higher mortality.
papers.corrections: No erratum, retraction or expression of concern in the PubMed record (no CommentsCorrections entries). Limitations to carry forward: troponin and echo results are not in the abstract, and complications are clinically coded (AF, HF, QTc, ischaemia) in older adults, so they do not equate to myocardial injury measured by biomarker.

papers.title: Assessment of Myocardial Function and Injury by Echocardiography and Cardiac Biomarkers in African Children With Severe Plasmodium falciparum Malaria.
papers.population_and_n: 104 children aged 3 months to 12 years with severe falciparum malaria (61 with severe malarial anaemia), Mbale Regional Referral Hospital, Uganda
papers.abstract_summary: This prospective study followed 104 Ugandan children with severe falciparum malaria, nested in the FEAST fluid-bolus trial context, with echocardiography at presentation and 24 hours. Cardiac troponin I and BNP were measured at presentation. Troponin I exceeded 0.1 ng/mL in 50 children (48%), while median BNP was normal. Cardiac index was higher in severe malarial anaemia than in other severe malaria (6.89 vs 5.28 L/min/m2) and normalised by 24 hours after transfusion and antimalarial treatment; it correlated inversely with haemoglobin. Only 4 children (3.8%) had depressed systolic function (EF <45%). Six died, and none developed pulmonary oedema or biventricular failure. The authors conclude that elevated cardiac index is a physiological response to anaemia, that systolic function is preserved in over 96%, and that troponin elevation does not correlate with cardiac dysfunction.
papers.key_finding: Troponin I was raised in 48% of children with severe malaria, yet systolic function was preserved in over 96% and troponin did not track dysfunction.
papers.corrections: No erratum, retraction or expression of concern in the PubMed record. The only CommentsCorrections entry is a published commentary (CommentIn, Pediatr Crit Care Med 2018;19(3):262-263, PMID 29499020). The abstract contains an apparent unit typo (haemoglobin '< 5 mg/dL', presumably g/dL) and 'n equals to 50' phrasing; these are transcription oddities, not corrections.

papers.title: Early high-sensitivity troponin elevation and short-term mortality in sepsis: a systematic review with meta-analysis.
papers.population_and_n: 17 studies, 6242 adults meeting Sepsis-3 criteria, with short-term mortality 16.9% to 53.8%
papers.abstract_summary: The review searched PubMed, Scopus and Embase for studies relating early high-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) to short-term mortality in adults with Sepsis-3 sepsis. Seventeen studies with 6242 patients were pooled with random-effects models. Non-survivors had higher hs-cTn than survivors (standardised mean difference 0.87, 95% CI 0.41-1.33). Elevated versus normal hs-cTn was associated with higher mortality (unadjusted OR 1.78, 95% CI 1.41-2.25). In studies that adjusted for confounders, the association disappeared (aOR 1.06, 95% CI 0.99-1.14). The authors conclude that troponin is raised in sepsis non-survivors and is linked to mortality, but is not an independent predictor of death, consistent with a marker of overall illness severity.
papers.key_finding: Raised hs-troponin in sepsis tracks mortality crudely (OR 1.78) but not after adjustment (aOR 1.06), so it behaves as a severity marker, not an independent predictor.
papers.corrections: No erratum, retraction or expression of concern in the PubMed record. The only CommentsCorrections entry is a published commentary (CommentIn, Crit Care 2025;29(1):118, PMID 40102885). Chosen over the 2023 meta-analysis (PMID 37773717, unadjusted HRs, older troponin assays, no Sepsis-3 restriction) because it separates crude from adjusted effects.

connections.shared_pathway: Parasite-burden-associated cardiac involvement in severe intraerythrocytic protozoal infection (hypoxic, inflammatory and possibly direct myocardial injury) that is linked to ICU-level illness and death.
connections.canine_evidence: CB014 (B. canis, 50 dogs vs 20 controls): ECG and echo changes were common but nonspecific, troponin I was raised in 19/50, CK-MB in all, and values were highest in the two dogs that died. CB146 (European canine babesiosis necropsies): haemorrhage, pericardial effusion, monocytic leukostasis, oedema, necrosis, congestion and myocarditis. CB080 (6 fatal B. canis cases): cardiomyocyte necrosis with multi-organ congestion and oedema. CB032 (single Boerboel): myocardial haemorrhage.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 35983604: 32 of 163 (19.6%) hospitalised babesiosis patients had a cardiac complication (AF, heart failure, QTc prolongation, ischaemia), and these patients had more parasitaemia >10%, longer ICU stay and higher mortality. PMID 33724926 (malaria SR/MA, not selected as a core paper) reports myocarditis and parasitised red cells in the myocardium at autopsy, and cardiac biomarker abnormalities in 0-57% of children.
connections.differences: Human babesiosis data are clinical diagnoses from older adults with comorbidity and frequent splenic or immune compromise (mainly B. microti), with no troponin in the abstract; canine data are mostly young dogs with B. canis or B. rossi and rely on biomarker plus necropsy. The canine histology (myocarditis, necrosis) has no human babesiosis pathology counterpart in the retrieved evidence. Treatment, timing of sampling and survivorship bias (necropsy series include only deaths) differ. Association with high parasitaemia and death is shown in humans, not mechanism.
connections.strength_rationale: Both hosts show cardiac involvement tracking severity and death, but the human babesiosis paper measures clinical cardiac diagnoses rather than myocardial injury, and the canine paper measures biomarkers and pathology, so the same mechanism was not measured in both.

connections.shared_pathway: Troponin release (myocardial injury) that is dissociated from overt systolic pump failure in severe parasitaemic disease.
connections.canine_evidence: CB014: troponin I raised in 19/50 dogs while ECG/echo abnormalities were described as common but nonspecific; CB080 nonetheless proposes circulatory failure as the probable cause of death with cardiomyocyte necrosis at necropsy.
connections.human_evidence: PMID 29206727 (severe falciparum malaria, 104 Ugandan children): troponin I >0.1 ng/mL in 48%, normal median BNP, EF <45% in only 3.8%, high cardiac index in severe malarial anaemia normalising by 24 h, and no correlation between troponin and dysfunction. The authors argue the findings show injury without systolic failure, and that the high cardiac index is an anaemia-driven physiological response.
connections.differences: This is a malaria comparator, not babesiosis. Cohort is children with a high share of severe malarial anaemia, with haemodynamics reflecting FEAST-era transfusion and fluid management; dogs are of mixed age and phenotype. Troponin assays and cut-offs differ between human and canine platforms. P. falciparum cytoadherent microvascular sequestration (including in myocardium) is a distinct mechanism from Babesia; the digest does not show equivalent sequestration in B. canis, though CB146 reports monocytic leukostasis. Both studies are associational and cannot assign cause to the troponin rise.
connections.strength_rationale: Troponin I and echo or cardiac function were assessed in both hosts and both show injury marker elevation without clear systolic failure, but the canine abstract does not test correlation between troponin and function, and the causal mechanism (hypoxia, anaemia, inflammation, parasitised cells) is not demonstrated in either.

connections.shared_pathway: Troponin elevation as a marker of overall illness severity and outcome, rather than an independent prognostic signal, in systemic inflammatory critical illness with circulatory compromise.
connections.canine_evidence: CB014: troponin I and CK-MB were highest in the two dogs that died (very small number of deaths, no adjustment). CB080: circulatory failure proposed as probable cause of death in 6 fatal cases, with congestion, effusions and cardiomyocyte necrosis (descriptive, deaths only).
connections.human_evidence: PMID 39953561 (sepsis, 17 studies, 6242 adults): non-survivors had higher hs-cTn (SMD 0.87) and unadjusted OR 1.78 for mortality, but adjusted OR 1.06 (95% CI 0.99-1.14). PMID 35983604 shows cardiac complications in babesiosis cluster with high parasitaemia, ICU stay and death, in line with a severity-marker interpretation. PMID 41666444 (TriNetX, 2026, not selected as a core paper) links babesiosis-related sepsis with shock and higher mortality, though its abstract gives no troponin data.
connections.differences: Sepsis is a heterogeneous syndrome of bacterial and other aetiologies with vasoplegia, and Sepsis-3 populations are adult ICU or ED patients with hs-troponin assays. Canine babesiosis is a haemolytic protozoal disease where anaemia, hypoxia and endothelial or coagulation disturbance (see COA digest) may drive injury. Canine data lack any adjusted prognostic analysis and have only two deaths in CB014, so the sepsis result cannot be transferred. The meta-analysis pools observational studies with substantial heterogeneity in design.
connections.strength_rationale: The sepsis finding is a confounded prognostic association in a different disease, and the canine signal rests on two non-survivors without adjustment, so no equivalent analysis exists in dogs and the link is an analogy.

papers.title: Comparative Outcomes of Babesiosis in Immunocompromised and Nonimmunocompromised Hosts: A Multicenter Cohort Study.
papers.first_pub_date: 2025-01-28 (PubMed entry date; PubMed issue date field reads 2025 Dec 24)
papers.population_and_n: 225 adults with laboratory-confirmed babesiosis (mean age 66 y, 36% female), 2009-2023, multiple centres in the northeastern US. 112 had immunocompromise or asplenia/hyposplenia (ICAH) and 113 were immune-intact.
papers.abstract_summary: This multicentre retrospective cohort compared babesiosis outcomes in adults with immunocompromising conditions or asplenia/hyposplenia (ICAH, n=112) against immune-intact adults (n=113). ICAH patients had higher median peak parasitaemia (2.8% vs 0.9%, P<.0001). They also had more acute kidney injury (24% vs 11%), more ARDS (11% vs 4%), more packed red cell transfusion (31% vs 17%) and more exchange transfusion (18% vs 6%). Median treatment lasted 27 vs 10 days, and 43 days when both immunocompromise and asplenia were present. Twelve-month all-cause mortality was 7% vs 1% (P=.019) and recurrence 8% vs 0%. Haematological malignancy (OR 7.0) and B-cell-depleting therapy (OR 9.4) predicted recurrence. Follow-up smear and PCR did not reliably predict recurrence. The authors conclude that ICAH patients have more severe disease and more complications.
papers.key_finding: Immunocompromised or asplenic patients had higher peak parasitaemia, AKI, ARDS and 12-month mortality (7% vs 1%) than immune-intact patients; B-cell depletion and haematological malignancy predicted recurrence.
papers.corrections: PubMed CommentsCorrections list is empty (no erratum, retraction or update notice in the record, checked 2026-10-23). The PubMed PubDate (2025 Dec 24) is a Medline issue-date artefact. The record was entered in PubMed on 2025-01-28, so use that as first publication. The abstract was read from the efetch XML record. The ICAH group pools immunocompromise and asplenia/hyposplenia, so effects cannot be separated for asplenia alone.

papers.title: Pulmonary Manifestations of Babesiosis and Predictors of Mortality from a Quaternary Care Center in Westchester, New York.
papers.population_and_n: 147 hospitalised adults with confirmed babesiosis, Westchester Medical Center, New York, 2006-2023. 63 were severe, 41 went to ICU and 10 died.
papers.abstract_summary: This single-centre retrospective study reviewed 147 hospitalised adults with confirmed babesiosis (2006-2023). Of these, 63 had severe disease, 41 were admitted to ICU and 10 died. Logistic regression was used to find factors linked to severity and mortality. Respiratory symptoms occurred in 42% of cases and 55 patients had an abnormal chest radiograph. Among severe cases, 75% had parasitaemia of 10% or more. Severity was associated with age 70 or older, severe dyspnoea, radiographic abnormality, WBC above 5000, haemoglobin 8 g/dL or lower, and raised creatinine. Lyme seropositivity was found in 28%. Exchange transfusion did not correlate with outcome. Mortality was higher with age 70 or older, encephalopathy, acute kidney injury, severe dyspnoea, abnormal chest radiograph and intubation.
papers.key_finding: In 147 hospitalised adults, severity tracked with age >=70, high parasitaemia, anaemia (Hb <=8) and raised creatinine; mortality with age, encephalopathy, AKI, abnormal chest radiograph and intubation.
papers.corrections: PubMed CommentsCorrections list is empty (no erratum or retraction, checked 2026-10-23). Single-centre retrospective study with 10 deaths, so mortality predictors rest on very few events. The abstract does not state effect sizes, and the abstract's own phrase is that associations were found by logistic regression, so I did not check whether the models were multivariable. Published in an MDPI journal.

papers.title: Risk Factors for Severe Infection, Hospitalization, and Prolonged Antimicrobial Therapy in Patients with Babesiosis.
papers.journal: The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene
papers.population_and_n: 128 patients with smear- or real-time PCR-confirmed Babesia microti infection, collected over 16 years.
papers.abstract_summary: This study evaluated 128 patients with smear- or real-time PCR-confirmed B. microti infection over 16 years, aiming to define prognostic indicators of serious complications needing hospitalisation or prolonged therapy. Patients with asplenia or immunocompromising conditions were more likely to have severe infection, need hospitalisation, or receive prolonged antimicrobial courses (all P<0.01). Nausea or vomiting, diarrhoea and hyperbilirubinaemia (all P<0.01) were predictive of severe infection, hospitalisation and prolonged therapy. Patients with concurrent Lyme disease were less likely to need hospitalisation, and had similar severity and antibiotic duration compared with those without Lyme disease. The abstract reports P values rather than effect sizes.
papers.key_finding: In 128 B. microti patients, asplenia or immunocompromise, GI symptoms and hyperbilirubinaemia predicted severe infection, hospitalisation and prolonged therapy; concurrent Lyme reduced hospitalisation.
papers.corrections: PubMed CommentsCorrections list is empty (no erratum or retraction, checked 2026-10-23). Chosen as the older, smaller supplement to the two 2025 papers because it is the only candidate that links asplenia/immunocompromise and hyperbilirubinaemia (a haemolysis/liver marker) to severity in one primary cohort. It is a 2017 study with n=128, and the abstract reports only P values (no effect sizes) and no parasitaemia analysis.

connections.shared_pathway: Loss of splenic function (asplenia or splenectomy) removes the main site of clearance of parasitised erythrocytes, which gives high parasitaemia, severe haemolytic disease and prolonged or relapsing infection.
connections.canine_evidence: CB021 (B. vogeli, experimental, n=6): intact Beagles had mild disease then prolonged subclinical infection, while splenectomised dogs developed severe, life-threatening anaemia and thrombocytopenia. CB120 (single case): a splenectomised, immunosuppressed dog with haemotropic Mycoplasma co-infection developed severe B. vulpes disease and was euthanised. CB116 (B. vogeli superinfection in E. canis-exposed Beagles): splenectomy raised E. canis loads. CB087 (n=187 infected dogs vs 15 controls): histology showed splenomegaly, rupture and circulatory disorder, which describes splenic involvement but not function. The canine experiments are small, and the other canine items are a case report and a descriptive series.
connections.human_evidence: 39873391: patients with asplenia/hyposplenia or immunocompromise (n=112 of 225) had higher peak parasitaemia (2.8% vs 0.9%), more AKI (24% vs 11%), more ARDS (11% vs 4%), longer treatment (median 43 days with both immunocompromise and asplenia), and 12-month mortality 7% vs 1%. 28722598: asplenia or immunocompromise predicted severe infection, hospitalisation and prolonged therapy (P<0.01, n=128).
connections.differences: The human data are retrospective associations in older, mostly northeastern US adults infected with B. microti. Asplenia/hyposplenia is pooled with immunocompromise in 39873391, so the spleen effect cannot be isolated. Canine splenectomy is a controlled experimental exposure in healthy young Beagles with B. vogeli, a low-virulence species. Natural canine splenic disease is mostly spleen enlargement rather than absence. B. rossi and B. canis are virulent in intact dogs, so spleen loss is not needed for severe canine disease, whereas B. microti is usually mild in immunocompetent humans. Mechanism (splenic filtration) is inferred in both hosts and was not directly measured in these papers.
connections.strength_rationale: The same exposure (no functional spleen) and the same outcome class (severe disease or high burden) are measured in both hosts, and the canine data are experimental. This is demonstrated for the exposure-outcome relationship, not for the splenic mechanism itself, which is inferred.

connections.shared_pathway: Impaired adaptive immunity (T-cell or B-cell deficiency, immunosuppressive therapy) leads to uncontrolled parasitaemia, severe disease and relapse.
connections.canine_evidence: CB008 (B. rossi, n=44 infected, 5 controls): complicated cases had lower CD3+ and CD4+ lymphocyte percentages than controls and uncomplicated dogs, which the authors read as functional immune suppression. CB120 (single case): a splenectomised, immunosuppressed dog with B. vulpes died. CB052 (B. rossi, endemic free-roaming dogs): 31% of 109 dogs were seropositive but healthy, and the confirmed cases were mostly mild, consistent with acquired immunity. CB141 (B. canis, n=342): antibody level correlated inversely with haematological severity, and autochthonous dogs were more severe and immunologically naive. None of these studies tested drug-induced immunosuppression or B-cell depletion in dogs.
connections.human_evidence: 39873391: immunocompromised or asplenic patients had higher peak parasitaemia, higher 12-month mortality and recurrence (8% vs 0%); haematological malignancy (OR 7.0) and B-cell-depleting therapy (OR 9.4) predicted recurrence. 28722598: immunocompromising conditions predicted severe infection and prolonged therapy.
connections.differences: Canine immune-deficit data are associational: lymphocyte subsets in sick dogs, or antibody in naive vs exposed dogs. They do not test iatrogenic B-cell depletion, haematological malignancy or transplant, which drive the human findings. Canine lymphopenia during acute babesiosis may be a consequence of severe inflammation rather than a pre-existing susceptibility. Human relapse follows prolonged persistence under B-cell depletion, while canine relapse data here come mainly from B. gibsoni, which is not cleared by treatment (CB094, CB067). The human cohorts also have comorbidity and polypharmacy confounding.
connections.strength_rationale: Both hosts link weaker adaptive immunity to worse outcomes, but the canine evidence is indirect (CD4 depletion in complicated disease, antibody inversely related to severity, one immunosuppressed case) and no canine study measures the human exposure (B-cell depletion) or the recurrence endpoint.

connections.shared_pathway: Parasite burden relates to the degree of haemolysis and the severity grade; high parasitaemia marks the severe, organ-dysfunction end of the spectrum.
connections.canine_evidence: CB141 (B. canis, n=342, subsets with parasitaemia data): parasitaemia and CRP correlated positively with haematological severity. CB123 (B. canis, n=61): young dogs had higher parasitaemia and more severe anaemia. CB073 (B. canis, n=54): parasite load and acute-phase proteins were not independent associates of SIRS, while leukopenia and monocytopenia were. So the canine association is clear for anaemia but not for the systemic inflammatory endpoint.
connections.human_evidence: 40333147: 75% of the 63 severe cases had parasitaemia of 10% or more, and haemoglobin of 8 g/dL or lower was associated with severe disease. 39873391: patients with higher complication rates (AKI, ARDS, transfusion) also had higher peak parasitaemia (2.8% vs 0.9%).
connections.differences: Parasitaemia is read from a smear in both hosts but is not standardised across them. Human parasitaemia thresholds (5% and 10%) are used clinically for exchange transfusion decisions, so selection bias and treatment effects enter the human data. Canine severity is graded as complicated vs uncomplicated or by MODS and SIRS, which is a different scale. B. rossi and B. canis hit very high parasitaemia less often than B. microti does in splenectomised hosts; B. rossi severity partly reflects an inflammatory response out of proportion to burden. Sequestration and microthrombosis (shown in B. rossi, CB145) differ from the human B. microti picture, and P. falciparum-type cytoadherence does not apply to either Babesia.
connections.strength_rationale: Parasitaemia and a severity outcome are measured and found to be positively associated in both hosts. This is rated with caution because the canine evidence is mixed (CB073 negative for SIRS), the canine severity endpoint in CB141 is haematological, and the human data are unadjusted descriptive associations.

connections.shared_pathway: Acute kidney injury and respiratory failure (ARDS, pulmonary oedema) as organ-dysfunction endpoints that mark and predict death.
connections.canine_evidence: CB025 (B. rossi, n=152): renal azotaemia in 14% was associated with collapse, hypoglycaemia, cerebral babesiosis, ARDS and lower survival, and was often missed by urine specific gravity. CB061 (B. canis, n=240): creatinine >5 mg/dL, phosphate >3 mmol/L and albumin <2.2 g/dL were associated with death, with 33.9% mortality when the kidney was involved. CB043 (smear-positive dogs, n=85): MODS in 15.3% with recovery of 38.4% vs 81.6% for uncomplicated disease. CB074 (B. gibsoni): urea, ALT and lactate predicted death. CB032 and CB097 (single necropsies): pulmonary oedema and glomerular lesions. CB040 (B. rossi, n=320): no independent multivariate predictor emerged.
connections.human_evidence: 40333147: mortality was higher with age >=70, encephalopathy, AKI, severe dyspnoea, abnormal chest radiograph and intubation (10 deaths in 147); creatinine rise and radiograph abnormality were associated with severe disease; respiratory symptoms in 42%. 39873391: AKI 24% vs 11% and ARDS 11% vs 4% in immunocompromised/asplenic vs immune-intact patients.
connections.differences: Canine kidney injury in B. rossi and B. canis includes documented glomerular and tubular injury (CB001, CB053) and haemoglobinuria. Human data are mostly clinical AKI without histology. Canine mortality is partly euthanasia-driven, whereas human deaths follow ICU care. Human cohorts are older (median ~66-71 y) with cardiac and renal comorbidity, which dogs lack. The human mortality predictors come from 10 events and are unlikely to be independent, similar to CB040, where univariable associations did not survive multivariate analysis.
connections.strength_rationale: The same organ-dysfunction endpoints (renal injury, pulmonary failure) are measured and tied to severity and death in both hosts. Evidence strength is limited by retrospective design, small event numbers in the human cohort, and unadjusted associations in several canine studies.

connections.shared_pathway: Haemolysis and hepatic/biochemical markers (bilirubin, anaemia depth) as indicators of severity.
connections.canine_evidence: CB040 (B. rossi, n=320): high bilirubin, urea, cortisol and low T4 discriminated best for death, although no independent multivariate predictors emerged. CB099 (n=81): 90% hyperbilirubinaemic, 82% anaemic. CB074 (B. gibsoni): urea, ALT and lactate were prognostic. CB067 (B. gibsoni, n=145): RBC <2x10^6/ul and persistent anaemia raised recurrence risk.
connections.human_evidence: 28722598: hyperbilirubinaemia, nausea/vomiting and diarrhoea predicted severe infection, hospitalisation and prolonged therapy (P<0.01). 40333147: haemoglobin of 8 g/dL or lower was associated with severe disease.
connections.differences: Bilirubin in dogs reflects haemolysis, cholestasis and hepatic injury and has no established cutoff comparable to the human series. The human bilirubin finding is univariable with P values only in a small 2017 cohort. Canine marker panels include lactate, cortisol and thyroid hormones, which none of the human papers tested. Secondary IMHA (CB067, CB153) has a human counterpart only as post-babesiosis autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, not covered by these papers.
connections.strength_rationale: Haemolysis and bilirubin markers are measured in both hosts, but the evidence is univariable and not independently confirmed in either (CB040 found no independent predictor, and 28722598 gives only P values), so the shared prognostic utility is plausible rather than demonstrated.

connections.shared_pathway: Age and co-infection as modifiers of severity.
connections.canine_evidence: CB043: older age associated with severe disease (MODS). CB123 (B. canis, n=61): young dogs had more severe anaemia and leukopenia and higher parasitaemia, which is the opposite direction. CB060 (B. vogeli +/- E. canis, n=44): co-infected dogs had lower RBC, Hb and Hct. CB116 (experimental): B. vogeli superinfection in E. canis-exposed Beagles gave worse anaemia and thrombocytopenia. CB126 (B. rossi, n=150): no haematological variable differed with E. canis co-infection (only 3 co-infected). CB109: co-infected dogs had milder ALP, urea and creatinine changes.
connections.human_evidence: 40333147: age >=70 was associated with severe disease and with death. 28722598: concurrent Lyme disease did not worsen severity and was associated with less hospitalisation.
connections.differences: Human risk concentrates in older adults with comorbidity and immune senescence. Canine age effects are inconsistent between studies and confounded by breed and naive immune status in young dogs. Human co-infection is with Borrelia, which is transmitted by the same Ixodes tick, while canine co-infections are with other haemoparasites (E. canis, D. repens, Hepatozoon). Canine co-infection results are mixed (CB060, CB116 worse; CB126, CB109 no change or milder), and the human Lyme data are a single-cohort finding.
connections.strength_rationale: Canine age and co-infection findings point in conflicting directions, the co-infecting organisms are not comparable, and the human evidence is one cohort association each. There is no shared mechanism that has been measured in both hosts.
